# 12-Week Strength & Conditioning Programme

**Client Profile:** Female, 47 | Advanced Lifter | Early Perimenopause
**Start Date:** 1 June 2026
**Programme Duration:** 12 weeks (ends 21 August 2026)

---

## Preamble: Clinical & Physiological Context

Before the programme structure, it is worth articulating the reasoning that shapes every decision here, so you can explain it clearly to your client.

**Perimenopause and training load.** Fluctuating and declining oestrogen directly affects tendon stiffness, collagen synthesis, and recovery capacity. Your client is advanced, so her neuromuscular competence is high, but her connective tissue is operating in a different hormonal environment than it was five years ago. This means progressive overload remains entirely appropriate — and is actively protective for bone density — but recovery windows need to be respected more deliberately than they might have been in her thirties.

**Vasomotor symptoms and exercise.** Hot flashes are triggered by a narrowed thermoneutral zone in the hypothalamus. Exercise raises core temperature, which can precipitate or worsen flashes. The restrictions the GP has flagged (no sauna, no fasted HIIT in heat) reflect this. The programme therefore builds structured cooling into every session as a non-negotiable component, schedules higher-intensity work earlier in the day where possible, avoids prolonged cardiovascular work in warm environments, and keeps rest periods long enough that core temperature can partially recover between sets.

**Cycle irregularity.** With a 23–52 day cycle range, you cannot reliably programme around follicular and luteal phases in the traditional sense. Instead, the programme uses a subjective daily readiness check (described below) to allow your client to modulate load on any given day. The structure is built around a consistent weekly skeleton, but intensity is expressed as a range, and she has explicit permission — and instruction — to train at the lower end of that range on days when symptoms are high.

---

## Readiness & Symptom Tracking Protocol

Ask your client to complete a brief check-in before every session. This takes under two minutes and gives you actionable data.

**Rate each item 1–5 (1 = very poor/severe, 5 = excellent/none):**

1. Sleep quality last night
2. Energy level right now
3. Hot flash severity in the last 24 hours
4. Joint comfort (particularly hips, knees, shoulders)
5. Mood / motivation

**Scoring:**
- **20–25:** Train as programmed. Full intensity range available.
- **13–19:** Train at the lower end of prescribed intensity. Reduce top sets by 5–10%. Prioritise technique and volume over load.
- **Below 13:** Reduce to movement-quality session only. Drop to 60–65% of working weights, cut volume by one-third, extend rest periods. Do not push through.

This is not a soft option — it is evidence-informed load management. Reinforce this with your client regularly.

---

## Cooling Protocol (Every Session, Non-Negotiable)

Given the heat intolerance and vasomotor symptoms, the following applies to all sessions regardless of phase or intensity:

**Before the session:**
- Client arrives or changes in a cool environment (ideally air-conditioned gym).
- Cold water bottle (500 ml minimum, ideally chilled) present at all times.
- Cooling towel (evaporative type) available at the bench or rack.
- Session scheduled before 11:00 am or after 17:00 pm during June–August to avoid peak ambient heat where possible.

**During the session:**
- Rest periods are a minimum of 2 minutes for compound lifts, 90 seconds for accessories. These are not optional. Use the rest period to sip cold water and apply the cooling towel to the back of the neck or wrists if a flash occurs.
- If a hot flash occurs mid-set, the set is paused or abandoned. The load is not increased on the next set. Resume when comfortable.
- Fan or air conditioning in the training space is strongly preferred. If training outdoors or in a warm space, reduce working loads by 10% across the board.

**After the session:**
- 10-minute cool-down walk in a cool environment or with a fan.
- Cold shower or cool-water face and neck wash within 20 minutes of finishing.
- Rehydration: minimum 500 ml water with electrolytes (sodium, magnesium) within 30 minutes post-session.

---

## Nutrition Framework

You noted nutrition as a component. The following is a framework for you to discuss with your client and, where appropriate, refer to a registered dietitian for individualisation.

**Protein.** This is the single most important nutritional lever for a perimenopausal advanced lifter. Declining oestrogen reduces muscle protein synthesis efficiency, meaning she needs more dietary protein than a younger woman doing the same programme. Target **1.8–2.2 g per kg of bodyweight per day**, distributed across at least four meals or eating occasions. No single meal should carry more than 40–45 g of protein, as leucine-triggered MPS has a ceiling effect per meal. Emphasise leucine-rich sources: eggs, dairy (particularly Greek yoghurt and cottage cheese), meat, fish, legumes combined with grains.

**Carbohydrates and training fuel.** The restriction on fasted HIIT in heat is noted. More broadly, your client should not train fasted for any high-intensity session in this programme. A small pre-session meal or snack containing 20–30 g of carbohydrate and 15–20 g of protein, consumed 60–90 minutes before training, will support performance and reduce the cortisol spike that fasted training produces — cortisol elevation is already a concern in perimenopause due to its interaction with oestrogen and progesterone fluctuation.

**Calcium and Vitamin D.** Given the bone density context, ensure she is meeting calcium needs through diet (1,000–1,200 mg/day from food sources: dairy, fortified plant milks, leafy greens, tinned fish with bones) and that her Vitamin D status has been checked by her GP. If supplementing, 1,000–2,000 IU D3 daily with a fat-containing meal is standard, but defer to her GP on specific dosing.

**Magnesium.** Magnesium glycinate or magnesium threonate (200–400 mg) taken in the evening has reasonable evidence for improving sleep quality and may modestly reduce vasomotor symptom frequency. This is worth raising with her GP as a low-risk adjunct.

**Hydration.** Vasomotor symptoms increase fluid loss. She should aim for pale-yellow urine throughout the day. On training days, add 500–750 ml above her usual intake. Cold fluids are preferable to warm during and after training.

**What to avoid around training.** Caffeine can lower the hot flash threshold in some women. If she uses pre-workout caffeine, suggest she monitors whether it correlates with increased flash frequency and consider shifting caffeine intake to earlier in the day or reducing dose.

---

## Programme Architecture

The 12 weeks are divided into three four-week phases, each with a distinct emphasis. The weekly training structure is consistent throughout: **four resistance sessions per week**, with two optional low-intensity conditioning sessions. The resistance sessions follow an upper/lower split with a power emphasis built into each phase.

**Weekly skeleton (consistent across all 12 weeks):**

| Day | Session |
|---|---|
| Monday | Lower Body — Strength Focus |
| Tuesday | Upper Body — Strength Focus |
| Wednesday | Optional: Low-Intensity Conditioning or Rest |
| Thursday | Lower Body — Power / Hypertrophy Focus |
| Friday | Upper Body — Power / Hypertrophy Focus |
| Saturday | Optional: Low-Intensity Conditioning or Active Recovery |
| Sunday | Rest |

The optional conditioning sessions are described at the end of each phase. They are genuinely optional — if vasomotor symptoms are high or sleep has been poor, rest is the better choice.

---

## Phase 1: Foundation & Adaptation (Weeks 1–4, 1 June – 28 June 2026)

### Phase Goals

The first four weeks establish movement quality under load, build connective tissue tolerance, and gather baseline data on how your client responds to the programme structure. Even for an advanced lifter, a foundation phase is not a step backward — it is an investment in the quality of the heavier work to come. You are also establishing the readiness check habit and the cooling protocol as normal parts of her training culture.

Intensity sits at **65–75% of estimated 1RM** for main lifts. Volume is moderate. Rest periods are generous. The emphasis is on bar speed, technique refinement, and building the habit of leaving something in the tank.

---

### Week 1 (1–7 June 2026)

**Monday — Lower Body Strength**

Begin with a thorough warm-up: 5 minutes of light cycling or rowing (cool environment), followed by hip 90/90 mobility, glute bridges, and two warm-up sets of the main lift at 40% and 55% of working weight.

*Main work:*
- Back Squat: 4 sets × 5 reps at 65% 1RM. Rest 3 minutes. Focus on controlled descent (3-second eccentric), pause at the bottom for 1 second, drive through the floor. The eccentric emphasis is deliberate — eccentric loading has the strongest evidence for bone density stimulus.
- Romanian Deadlift: 3 sets × 8 reps at 65% 1RM. Rest 2.5 minutes. Hinge pattern, feel the hamstring load, no rounding of the lumbar spine.
- Bulgarian Split Squat: 3 sets × 8 reps each leg, bodyweight or light dumbbells. Rest 2 minutes. This is a balance and unilateral stability exercise this week, not a loading exercise.
- Seated Calf Raise: 3 sets × 12 reps. Rest 90 seconds. Slow and controlled.
- Pallof Press: 3 sets × 10 reps each side. Rest 90 seconds. Anti-rotation core stability.

*Cool-down:* 5 minutes walking, hip flexor and hamstring stretching in a cool space.

**Tuesday — Upper Body Strength**

Warm-up: band pull-aparts × 20, shoulder CARs, two warm-up sets of pressing movement.

*Main work:*
- Barbell Bench Press: 4 sets × 5 reps at 65% 1RM. Rest 3 minutes. Full range, controlled descent, no bouncing off the chest.
- Barbell Bent-Over Row: 4 sets × 6 reps at 65% 1RM. Rest 2.5 minutes. Horizontal pull to balance the pressing volume.
- Seated Dumbbell Overhead Press: 3 sets × 8 reps. Rest 2 minutes. Seated to reduce spinal loading and core fatigue.
- Lat Pulldown (wide grip): 3 sets × 10 reps. Rest 2 minutes.
- Face Pull (cable, rope attachment): 3 sets × 15 reps. Rest 90 seconds. Rear delt and external rotator health — critical for long-term shoulder integrity.
- Tricep Pushdown: 3 sets × 12 reps. Rest 90 seconds.

**Wednesday — Optional Conditioning**

If energy and symptoms allow: 25–30 minutes of steady-state cycling, swimming, or walking at a conversational pace. Heart rate should stay below 130 bpm. Cool environment essential. This is not a workout — it is active recovery with a cardiovascular maintenance benefit.

**Thursday — Lower Body Power/Hypertrophy**

Warm-up as Monday.

*Main work:*
- Trap Bar Deadlift: 4 sets × 5 reps at 70% 1RM. Rest 3 minutes. The trap bar reduces shear force on the lumbar spine and allows a more upright torso — a good choice for this phase.
- Leg Press: 3 sets × 10 reps at moderate load. Rest 2 minutes. Higher foot placement to emphasise glutes and hamstrings.
- Walking Lunge: 3 sets × 10 reps each leg, bodyweight. Rest 2 minutes.
- Nordic Hamstring Curl (or lying leg curl): 3 sets × 6–8 reps. Rest 2 minutes. Eccentric hamstring loading for tendon health.
- Glute Bridge with Barbell: 3 sets × 12 reps. Rest 90 seconds.
- Dead Bug: 3 sets × 8 reps each side. Rest 90 seconds.

**Friday — Upper Body Power/Hypertrophy**

Warm-up as Tuesday.

*Main work:*
- Incline Dumbbell Press: 4 sets × 8 reps. Rest 2.5 minutes.
- Cable Row (seated, neutral grip): 4 sets × 8 reps. Rest 2.5 minutes.
- Arnold Press: 3 sets × 10 reps. Rest 2 minutes.
- Chest-Supported Dumbbell Row: 3 sets × 10 reps. Rest 2 minutes.
- Dumbbell Lateral Raise: 3 sets × 15 reps. Rest 90 seconds.
- Bicep Curl (EZ bar): 3 sets × 12 reps. Rest 90 seconds.
- Cable Tricep Overhead Extension: 3 sets × 12 reps. Rest 90 seconds.

**Saturday — Optional Active Recovery**

Yoga, gentle mobility work, or a 20-minute walk. No intensity. Focus on parasympathetic recovery.

---

### Weeks 2–4 (8–28 June 2026)

This approach has good evidence for maintaining fast-twitch muscle fibre recruitment, which declines with age and is particularly important for fall prevention and functional power in perimenopausal women.

Note that late June through July is the hottest part of the year in the Northern Hemisphere. The cooling protocol becomes even more important during this phase. # Nutrition Plan: Perimenopause & Bone Health Support

**Integrated with 12-Week Programme | Start Date: 1 June 2026**

---

## Foundational Philosophy

Before presenting specific targets and meal structures, it is worth being explicit about the nutritional logic underpinning every recommendation here. Your client is navigating three overlapping nutritional challenges simultaneously, and understanding how they interact will help you explain the plan to her in a way that feels coherent rather than like a list of rules.

**Challenge one: muscle protein synthesis efficiency is declining.** Oestrogen plays a direct role in anabolic signalling. As oestrogen fluctuates and trends downward in perimenopause, the muscle protein synthesis response to a given dose of dietary protein becomes blunted. This is sometimes called anabolic resistance. The practical consequence is that she needs more protein than she did in her thirties, distributed more deliberately across the day, to achieve the same muscle-building and muscle-preserving stimulus.

**Challenge two: bone remodelling is accelerating in the wrong direction.** Oestrogen suppresses osteoclast activity — the cells that break down bone. As oestrogen declines, osteoclasts become relatively more active, and bone resorption outpaces bone formation. Resistance training is the most powerful non-pharmacological intervention available to counter this, which is why the GP cleared her for full resistance training. But nutrition is the essential substrate: without adequate calcium, vitamin D, protein, magnesium, vitamin K2, and phosphorus, the bone-building stimulus from training cannot be fully realised. The skeleton cannot build what it is not given the materials to build.

**Challenge three: vasomotor symptoms create secondary nutritional disruption.** Hot flashes disturb sleep. Poor sleep elevates cortisol. Elevated cortisol increases appetite for energy-dense foods, promotes fat storage particularly around the abdomen, and impairs recovery from training. Certain dietary patterns — high refined sugar intake, excessive caffeine, alcohol, spicy foods — are well-documented hot flash triggers in susceptible women. The nutrition plan therefore addresses not just macronutrients and micronutrients but also the dietary patterns that modulate symptom frequency and severity.

These three challenges are addressed together, not separately. A high-protein, nutrient-dense, anti-inflammatory dietary pattern serves all three simultaneously.

---

## Caloric Framework

### Establishing Energy Needs

For an advanced lifter in perimenopause training four days per week, a reasonable starting estimate for total daily energy expenditure (TDEE) uses the Mifflin-St Jeor equation adjusted for activity level. Without your client's specific bodyweight, the following framework uses a placeholder of **70 kg** — adjust all figures proportionally for her actual weight.

**Estimated Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) at 70 kg, 47 years, female:**
Approximately 1,420–1,480 kcal/day.

**Activity multiplier:** With four resistance sessions per week plus optional conditioning, an activity factor of 1.55 (moderately active) is appropriate, giving a TDEE of approximately **2,200–2,300 kcal/day**.

### Caloric Target by Goal

This programme is not a fat loss programme — it is a strength, bone health, and symptom management programme. Aggressive caloric restriction during perimenopause is counterproductive: it accelerates muscle loss, worsens cortisol elevation, impairs bone remodelling, and frequently worsens vasomotor symptoms. The caloric target should therefore be set at or very close to maintenance.

**Recommended caloric target: 2,100–2,300 kcal/day on training days.**

On rest days, appetite will naturally be somewhat lower. A modest reduction of 150–200 kcal on rest days is acceptable and does not need to be forced — simply following hunger cues on rest days will usually achieve this naturally for most women.

**What to avoid:** Do not allow your client to drop below 1,800 kcal/day on any day, including rest days. Below this threshold, protein targets become very difficult to meet, micronutrient intake suffers, and the hormonal environment becomes more catabolic. If body composition change is a secondary goal, address it through the quality and composition of calories rather than aggressive restriction.

---

## Macronutrient Targets

### Protein: The Priority Macronutrient

**Daily target: 1.8–2.2 g per kg bodyweight.**
At 70 kg, this is **126–154 g of protein per day.**

Round to a practical working target of **140 g/day** as a minimum, with 150–155 g on training days being ideal.

This is higher than general population recommendations and higher than many standard sports nutrition guidelines. The elevation is justified by the anabolic resistance of perimenopause and the bone health context — dietary protein provides the amino acid substrate for collagen synthesis in bone matrix, and higher protein intakes are associated with better bone mineral density outcomes in postmenopausal and perimenopausal women in the literature.

**Distribution matters as much as total intake.** Muscle protein synthesis is maximised when leucine threshold is reached at each meal — approximately 2.5–3 g of leucine per eating occasion, which corresponds to roughly 30–40 g of high-quality protein. Spreading 140 g across four eating occasions (breakfast, lunch, pre-training snack or post-training meal, dinner) achieves this far more effectively than eating 50 g at dinner and smaller amounts earlier in the day.

**Practical protein distribution across the day:**

| Meal | Protein Target | Example Sources |
|---|---|---|
| Breakfast | 30–35 g | 3 eggs + 150 g Greek yoghurt, or protein oats with cottage cheese |
| Lunch | 35–40 g | 150 g chicken breast + legumes, or 180 g salmon + quinoa |
| Pre/Post Training | 25–30 g | Protein shake + milk, or cottage cheese + fruit |
| Dinner | 35–40 g | 150–180 g lean meat or fish + vegetables |

**On protein quality.** Leucine content varies significantly between protein sources. Animal proteins (meat, fish, eggs, dairy) are generally leucine-rich and complete. Plant proteins are not inferior, but they require larger quantities or strategic combining to reach the same leucine threshold per meal. If your client eats a predominantly plant-based diet, target the upper end of the protein range (2.2 g/kg) and ensure she includes soy, edamame, tempeh, and lentils as primary sources, as these have the highest leucine content among plant foods.

**Protein timing around training.** The anabolic window is wider than was once believed, but timing still matters for an advanced lifter. Aim for a protein-containing meal or snack within 2 hours before training and within 2 hours after training. The pre-training meal also serves the function of preventing fasted training, which is explicitly contraindicated in this programme.

---

### Carbohydrates: Fuel, Recovery, and Symptom Management

**Daily target: 3.5–4.5 g per kg bodyweight on training days.**
At 70 kg, this is **245–315 g/day on training days.**

**On rest days: 2.5–3.5 g per kg bodyweight**, approximately **175–245 g/day.**

Carbohydrates are not the enemy in perimenopause, despite the cultural noise around low-carbohydrate diets for women in midlife. Adequate carbohydrate intake supports training performance, maintains muscle glycogen, supports thyroid function (which is already under pressure from hormonal fluctuation), and helps regulate cortisol. Chronically low carbohydrate intake in a woman doing four resistance sessions per week will impair recovery and worsen fatigue.

**Carbohydrate quality is the key variable.** The emphasis should be on complex, fibre-rich carbohydrates with a low to moderate glycaemic index. These support stable blood glucose, which in turn supports mood stability and reduces the cortisol spikes that worsen vasomotor symptoms. Refined carbohydrates and high-sugar foods cause rapid blood glucose fluctuations that can trigger or worsen hot flashes in some women.

**Preferred carbohydrate sources:**
- Oats, quinoa, brown rice, sweet potato, wholegrain bread and pasta
- Legumes (lentils, chickpeas, black beans) — these also contribute meaningfully to protein intake
- Fruit, particularly berries (high in antioxidants and phytoestrogens)
- Root vegetables (parsnip, beetroot, carrot)

**Carbohydrate timing:** Prioritise carbohydrates around training. A carbohydrate-containing pre-training meal (60–90 minutes before) fuels the session. A carbohydrate-containing post-training meal replenishes glycogen and supports the insulin-mediated uptake of amino acids into muscle. Evening carbohydrates are not problematic and may actually support sleep quality by facilitating serotonin and melatonin synthesis — this is worth communicating to your client if she has been avoiding carbohydrates at dinner based on popular advice.

**Phytoestrogens deserve a specific mention.** Soy isoflavones and lignans (found in flaxseed, sesame seeds, and wholegrains) are weak oestrogen receptor agonists. The evidence for their effect on vasomotor symptoms is modest but consistent — regular consumption of soy foods (not supplements) is associated with a small but meaningful reduction in hot flash frequency in some women. Encourage your client to include edamame, tofu, tempeh, or soy milk regularly if she is not already doing so. This is a food-first recommendation, not a supplement recommendation.

---

### Fat: Hormonal Substrate and Anti-Inflammatory Function

**Daily target: 25–30% of total calories from fat.**
At 2,200 kcal/day, this is approximately **61–73 g of fat per day.**

Dietary fat is the substrate for steroid hormone synthesis, including the residual oestrogen production that occurs in adipose tissue during perimenopause. Very low fat diets are inappropriate for perimenopausal women. The emphasis should be on the quality and type of fat rather than restriction.

**Omega-3 fatty acids are the priority.** EPA and DHA (found in oily fish) have anti-inflammatory effects that are relevant to joint health, cardiovascular health, and potentially to vasomotor symptom severity. Some evidence suggests omega-3 supplementation may modestly reduce hot flash frequency. Target **two to three portions of oily fish per week** (salmon, mackerel, sardines, herring, trout). If your client does not eat fish, algae-based omega-3 supplements (which provide EPA and DHA directly, unlike flaxseed which provides ALA) are the appropriate alternative.

**Preferred fat sources:**
- Oily fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines)
- Extra virgin olive oil — primary cooking and dressing fat
- Avocado
- Nuts (particularly walnuts for omega-3 content, almonds for calcium)
- Seeds (flaxseed, chia, hemp — also provide lignans)
- Eggs (yolk contains fat-soluble vitamins D and K)

**Limit:** Saturated fat from processed sources (ultra-processed foods, pastries, processed meats). Modest amounts of saturated fat from whole food sources (dairy, eggs, unprocessed meat) are not a concern at the quantities present in this plan.

**Avoid:** Trans fats entirely. These are pro-inflammatory and have no place in a health-focused nutrition plan.

---

## Bone Health Micronutrient Protocol

This section is the most specific and most important for your client's long-term skeletal health. Each nutrient is addressed individually with rationale, food sources, and supplementation guidance where appropriate. All supplementation recommendations should be reviewed with her GP.

---

### Calcium: The Structural Mineral

**Target: 1,000–1,200 mg/day from food sources.**

Calcium is the primary mineral in hydroxyapatite, the crystalline structure that gives bone its compressive strength. During perimenopause, increased osteoclast activity means calcium is being released from bone at a higher rate. Adequate dietary calcium does not prevent this process, but inadequate dietary calcium forces the body to draw on skeletal stores to maintain serum calcium levels, accelerating bone loss.

**The food-first principle applies strongly here.** Calcium from food is absorbed more efficiently and with fewer risks than calcium from supplements. Calcium supplements (particularly calcium carbonate in high doses) have been associated in some studies with increased cardiovascular risk, though this remains debated. Food-sourced calcium does not carry this concern.

**Calcium-rich food sources and approximate content:**

| Food | Serving | Calcium (mg) |
|---|---|---|
| Plain Greek yoghurt | 200 g | 240–280 mg |
| Milk (dairy or fortified soy) | 250 ml | 280–300 mg |
| Cottage cheese | 200 g | 130–150 mg |
| Cheddar cheese | 30 g | 200–220 mg |
| Tinned sardines (with bones) | 100 g | 350–380 mg |
| Tinned salmon (with bones) | 100 g | 200–230 mg |
| Firm tofu (calcium-set) | 100 g | 200–350 mg |
| Edamame | 150 g | 100–130 mg |
| Kale (cooked) | 100 g | 150–180 mg |
| Broccoli (cooked) | 150 g | 60–80 mg |
| Almonds | 30 g | 75–80 mg |
| White beans | 150 g | 120–140 mg |
| Fortified orange juice | 250 ml | 280–300 mg |

**Building to 1,200 mg from food is achievable** with two to three dairy or fortified dairy-alternative servings per day plus regular inclusion of tinned fish with bones, leafy greens, and legumes. A sample day might include: Greek yoghurt at breakfast (260 mg), milk in coffee and cooking (150 mg), tinned sardines at lunch (360 mg), kale at dinner (160 mg), almonds as a snack (80 mg) — totalling approximately 1,010 mg before accounting for incidental calcium in other foods.

**Supplementation:** If dietary calcium consistently falls below 800 mg/day, a supplement of 200–400 mg calcium citrate (not carbonate — citrate is better absorbed and does not require stomach acid) taken with food is reasonable. Do not supplement more than 500 mg at a time, as absorption efficiency drops above this threshold. Discuss with GP.

**Calcium absorption inhibitors to be aware of:** Oxalates (in spinach, rhubarb, beet greens) bind calcium and reduce its absorption — these foods are not harmful, but they should not be relied upon as primary calcium sources. Phytates in wholegrains can similarly reduce calcium absorption, though the effect is modest in the context of a varied diet. Excess sodium increases urinary calcium excretion — another reason to moderate processed food intake.

---

### Vitamin D: The Absorption Gatekeeper

**Target: Serum 25(OH)D level of 75–120 nmol/L (30–48 ng/mL).**
**Supplementation: 1,000–2,000 IU vitamin D3 daily, with a fat-containing meal.**

Vitamin D is not a vitamin in the traditional sense — it is a steroid hormone precursor. Its role in calcium absorption is fundamental: without adequate vitamin D, only 10–15% of dietary calcium is absorbed from the gut. With adequate vitamin D, absorption rises to 30–40%. This means that a client with excellent calcium intake but poor vitamin D status is still at significant risk of calcium insufficiency at the tissue level.

Vitamin D status is almost universally suboptimal in the UK and Northern Europe, particularly in winter months and in individuals who spend limited time outdoors. Your client's programme starts in June, which is the best time of year for cutaneous vitamin D synthesis in the Northern Hemisphere — but this should not be relied upon as the primary source, particularly given the heat intolerance that may limit outdoor time.

**Dietary sources of vitamin D are limited:**

| Food | Serving | Vitamin D (IU) |
|---|---|---|
| Salmon (wild) | 100 g | 600–1,000 IU |
| Mackerel | 100 g | 400–500 IU |
| Sardines (tinned) | 100 g | 200–300 IU |
| Egg yolk | 1 large | 40–50 IU |
| Fortified milk | 250 ml | 100–120 IU |
| Fortified cereal | 30 g | 40–80 IU |

It is essentially impossible to meet optimal vitamin D needs through diet alone. Supplementation is appropriate and should be discussed with her GP, who can arrange a serum 25(OH)D test to establish baseline status and guide dosing. Standard supplementation of 1,000–2,000 IU D3 daily is safe for most adults without testing, but testing allows precise dosing.

**Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) is preferred over D2 (ergocalciferol)** — D3 is more effective at raising and maintaining serum levels.

**Take with the largest fat-containing meal of the day** — vitamin D is fat-soluble and absorption is significantly enhanced in the presence of dietary fat.

---

### Vitamin K2: The Calcium Director

**Target: 90–180 mcg/day of vitamin K2 (MK-7 form) from food and/or supplementation.**

Vitamin K2 is the least well-known of the bone health nutrients but arguably one of the most important in the context of perimenopause. Its primary role in bone health is the activation of osteocalcin, a protein produced by osteoblasts (bone-building cells) that binds calcium into bone matrix. Without adequate K2, osteocalcin remains inactive (undercarboxylated), and calcium is less effectively incorporated into bone even when calcium and vitamin D status are adequate.

There is also a cardiovascular dimension: K2 activates matrix Gla protein, which prevents calcium from depositing in arterial walls. This is relevant because calcium supplementation without adequate K2 may theoretically increase arterial calcification risk — another reason to prioritise food-sourced calcium and ensure K2 adequacy.

**Dietary sources of vitamin K2:**

| Food | Serving | K2 (mcg) |
|---|---|---|
| Natto (fermented soy) | 100 g | 800–1,000 mcg |
| Hard cheese (Gouda, Edam) | 30 g | 10–15 mcg |
| Soft cheese (Brie, Camembert) | 30 g | 5–10 mcg |
| Egg yolk | 1 large | 5–6 mcg |
| Butter (grass-fed) | 10 g | 2–3 mcg |
| Chicken liver | 100 g | 10–15 mcg |
| Sauerkraut | 100 g | 4–5 mcg |

Natto is by far the richest source but is an acquired taste. For most Western clients, reaching 90–180 mcg from food alone is challenging. A supplement of **100–200 mcg MK-7 (menaquinone-7)** daily is a practical and well-tolerated option. MK-7 has a longer half-life than MK-4 and is the preferred supplemental form. Take with a fat-containing meal alongside vitamin D3 — these two nutrients work synergistically.

**Important note for GP review:** Vitamin K2 at supplemental doses can interact with warfarin and other anticoagulant medications. Confirm your client is not on anticoagulants before recommending supplementation.

---

### Magnesium: The Overlooked Mineral

**Target: 320–400 mg/day from food, with supplementation if dietary intake is insufficient.**

Magnesium is involved in over 300 enzymatic reactions in the body. Its relevance here is threefold. First, approximately 60% of the body's magnesium is stored in bone, where it contributes to bone crystal structure and influences osteoblast and osteoclast activity. Low magnesium status is associated with lower bone mineral density. Second, magnesium is required for the conversion of vitamin D to its active form — magnesium deficiency can therefore impair vitamin D function even when vitamin D intake is adequate. Third, magnesium has well-documented effects on sleep quality and may modestly reduce vasomotor symptom frequency, both of which are directly relevant to your client.

**Dietary sources of magnesium:**

| Food | Serving | Magnesium (mg) |
|---|---|---|
| Pumpkin seeds | 30 g | 150–160 mg |
| Dark chocolate (85%+) | 30 g | 50–65 mg |
| Almonds | 30 g | 75–80 mg |
| Spinach (cooked) | 100 g | 80–90 mg |
| Black beans | 150 g | 90–100 mg |
| Edamame | 150 g | 60–70 mg |
| Quinoa (cooked) | 150 g | 60–70 mg |
| Salmon | 100 g | 30–35 mg |
| Avocado | 100 g | 25–30 mg |
| Banana | 1 medium | 30–35 mg |

A diet rich in nuts, seeds, legumes, and leafy greens can reach 300–350 mg/day. If dietary intake is consistently below 300 mg, supplementation with **200–400 mg magnesium glycinate or magnesium threonate** in the evening is appropriate. These forms are better absorbed and less likely to cause the gastrointestinal side effects (loose stools) associated with magnesium oxide or magnesium citrate at higher doses. Evening timing takes advantage of magnesium's relaxing effect on the nervous system to support sleep.

---

### Collagen and Vitamin C: Connective Tissue Support

**Target: 10–15 g hydrolysed collagen peptides + 50–100 mg vitamin C, taken 30–60 minutes before training.**

This recommendation sits at the intersection of bone health and tendon/ligament health. Collagen is the primary structural protein in bone matrix, tendons, and ligaments. Declining oestrogen reduces collagen synthesis, which is why perimenopausal women experience increased tendon injury risk and joint discomfort. Hydrolysed collagen peptides, taken with vitamin C (which is required as a cofactor for collagen synthesis), have emerging evidence for supporting connective tissue repair and may contribute to bone collagen matrix quality.

The timing recommendation — 30–60 minutes before training — is based on research showing that collagen synthesis is stimulated by exercise, and that pre-exercise collagen supplementation increases the availability of collagen precursors in the circulation during the training window.

This is a supplementation recommendation rather than a food-first recommendation, as achieving therapeutic doses of specific collagen peptides from food alone is impractical. Bone broth contains collagen but in variable and generally lower quantities than a standardised supplement. A good quality hydrolysed collagen powder (unflavoured or lightly flavoured) mixed into a pre-training drink or smoothie is the most practical delivery method.

---

### Omega-3 Fatty Acids: Anti-Inflammatory Foundation

**Target: 2–3 g combined EPA + DHA per day from food and/or supplementation.**

As noted in the macronutrient section, omega-3 fatty acids have anti-inflammatory effects relevant to joint health, cardiovascular health, and potentially vasomotor symptom severity. Two to three portions of oily fish per week provides approximately 1.5–2 g EPA + DHA on fish days but nothing on non-fish days. For consistent daily intake, supplementation with a high-quality fish oil or algae-based omega-3 providing 1–2 g EPA + DHA daily is appropriate.

**Take with the largest meal of the day** to improve absorption and reduce the fishy aftertaste that some clients find unpleasant.

## Preamble: Why Cardio Programming for This Client Is Not Straightforward

For most advanced lifters, adding a cardio maintenance block to a strength programme is relatively simple arithmetic: pick modalities, assign intensities, distribute across the week, manage fatigue. For your client, the calculus is more complex, and it is worth being explicit about why before presenting the structure.

**The thermoregulatory problem.** Cardiovascular exercise raises core temperature more rapidly and to a greater degree than resistance training, because the sustained nature of aerobic work does not allow the partial recovery between sets that resistance training provides. For a woman with a narrowed thermoneutral zone — which is precisely what vasomotor symptoms represent at a physiological level — this means cardio carries a higher risk of precipitating hot flashes mid-session than resistance training does. This is not a reason to avoid cardio. It is a reason to be precise about modality, intensity, environment, duration, and timing in a way that a trainer working with a younger client without vasomotor symptoms would not need to be.

**The cortisol problem.** Sustained moderate-to-high intensity cardiovascular exercise is a significant cortisol stimulus. In a hormonally stable younger woman, this cortisol spike is transient and well-managed. In perimenopause, where the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis is already under pressure from fluctuating oestrogen and progesterone, repeated high cortisol stimuli from cardio can worsen fatigue, disrupt sleep, increase abdominal fat deposition, and paradoxically worsen vasomotor symptoms. This does not mean cardio is harmful — it means the dose and intensity must be calibrated carefully.

**The recovery competition problem.** Your client is training four resistance sessions per week at progressive intensities. Cardio competes for recovery resources: glycogen, protein synthesis capacity, connective tissue repair, nervous system recovery. Adding too much cardio, or cardio at the wrong intensity, will compromise strength gains and increase injury risk. The cardio programme is therefore designed to complement the resistance programme, not compete with it.

**The opportunity.** Despite these constraints, cardio is genuinely important for this client. Cardiovascular fitness is independently protective against the cardiovascular disease risk that increases significantly after menopause. Aerobic exercise improves insulin sensitivity, which helps manage the body composition changes of perimenopause. Certain cardio modalities — particularly swimming and cycling — are joint-friendly and thermally manageable. And there is reasonable evidence that regular moderate aerobic exercise reduces vasomotor symptom frequency over time, even though individual sessions may temporarily trigger flashes. The goal is to build a sustainable cardio habit that delivers these benefits without the costs of poorly designed programming.

## Intensity Framework: Understanding the Three Zones

All cardio in this programme is assigned to one of three intensity zones. Understanding these zones precisely — not just approximately — is essential for managing the thermoregulatory and cortisol concerns described above.

### Zone 1: Low Intensity (Recovery and Aerobic Base)

**Heart rate: 50–60% of maximum heart rate (HRmax)**
**RPE: 2–3 out of 10 (very easy, fully conversational)**
**Perceived effort:** Could hold a full conversation without any breathlessness. Could sustain this indefinitely.

At 47 years old, estimated HRmax is approximately 173 bpm (using the formula 220 minus age). Zone 1 therefore corresponds to approximately **87–104 bpm**.

Zone 1 work is genuinely easy. Many clients underestimate how easy it should feel and drift into Zone 2 without realising it. Use a heart rate monitor to keep her honest. Zone 1 sessions are primarily recovery tools — they increase blood flow to muscles, support parasympathetic nervous system activity, and contribute to aerobic base without adding meaningful physiological stress. They are also the safest zone for vasomotor symptom management, as the core temperature rise is modest and gradual.

### Zone 2: Moderate Intensity (Aerobic Development)

**Heart rate: 60–75% of HRmax**
**RPE: 4–6 out of 10 (comfortable but requires attention, can speak in sentences but not freely)**
**Perceived effort:** Breathing is noticeably elevated but controlled. Could sustain for 30–60 minutes with effort.

At 47 years old, Zone 2 corresponds to approximately **104–130 bpm**.

Zone 2 is the primary aerobic development zone. It is where mitochondrial density increases, fat oxidation capacity improves, and cardiovascular efficiency develops. It is also the zone most associated with the long-term reduction in vasomotor symptom frequency seen in exercise intervention studies. The majority of your client's cardio volume will sit here.

Zone 2 carries a moderate core temperature rise and a moderate cortisol stimulus. Both are manageable with appropriate session length, environment, and cooling protocols. Sessions should not exceed 45 minutes in this zone during the programme, and the cooling protocol from the main programme applies in full.

### Zone 3: High Intensity (Threshold and Above)

**Heart rate: above 80% of HRmax**
**RPE: 7–9 out of 10 (hard to very hard, speech limited to single words or short phrases)**
**Perceived effort:** Breathing is heavy. Sustainable only for short intervals.

At 47 years old, Zone 3 begins at approximately **138 bpm**.

Zone 3 work — including traditional HIIT — carries the highest thermoregulatory risk, the highest cortisol stimulus, and the greatest competition with resistance training recovery. The GP restriction on fasted HIIT in heat reflects this. Zone 3 work is not excluded from this programme, but it is used sparingly, structured carefully, and subject to strict environmental and readiness conditions. It is never programmed on the same day as a heavy resistance session, never performed fasted, and never performed in a warm environment.

## Modality Selection and Rationale

Not all cardio modalities are equal for this client. The following assessment considers thermoregulatory load, joint impact, bone loading stimulus, and practical accessibility.

### Swimming: Preferred Modality for High-Symptom Days

Swimming is the single best cardio modality for a perimenopausal woman with significant vasomotor symptoms. The water provides continuous passive cooling of the skin surface, which directly counteracts the core temperature rise of exercise and dramatically reduces the likelihood of triggering a hot flash. Water temperature in most pools (26–28°C) is below skin temperature, creating a constant heat dissipation gradient that no other common exercise modality can replicate.

Swimming is also non-impact, making it joint-friendly and appropriate on days when lower body soreness from resistance training is present. It provides a genuine cardiovascular stimulus across all three zones and engages the upper body musculature in a way that complements rather than duplicates the resistance programme.

**The limitation of swimming** is that it provides no bone loading stimulus — the buoyancy of water eliminates the ground reaction forces that drive osteogenic adaptation. Swimming should therefore be understood as a cardiovascular tool, not a bone health tool. The resistance programme carries the bone loading responsibility.

**Practical note:** If your client does not have access to a pool, or if pool temperatures are too warm (some leisure centre pools are kept at 30°C or above, which reduces the cooling benefit), this modality should be deprioritised. Confirm pool temperature before scheduling.

### Cycling (Indoor): Preferred Modality for Controlled Intensity

Indoor cycling on a stationary bike or smart trainer offers precise intensity control, a cool environment (assuming air-conditioned gym or home setup with a fan), and zero impact on the lower body joints. It is the most controllable cardio modality for Zone 2 work, as power output can be set precisely and heart rate response monitored continuously.

The seated position means core temperature rise is somewhat lower than running at equivalent heart rates, because less muscle mass is engaged and there is less postural work. This makes indoor cycling a good choice for longer Zone 2 sessions.

**The limitation** is that cycling is non-weight-bearing and therefore provides no bone loading stimulus, similar to swimming. It also places the hip flexors in a shortened position for extended periods, which can create tightness that affects squat and deadlift mechanics — worth monitoring and addressing with hip flexor mobility work in warm-ups.

### Rowing (Indoor): High Value, Moderate Thermoregulatory Load

The rowing ergometer is an excellent full-body cardiovascular tool that engages approximately 86% of muscle mass, making it highly efficient for cardiovascular development. It is non-impact and provides a meaningful posterior chain stimulus that complements the resistance programme.

The limitation for this client is that rowing at moderate-to-high intensity generates significant heat due to the large muscle mass involved. It is appropriate for Zone 1 and lower Zone 2 work but should be used cautiously for longer or more intense sessions. A fan directed at the rower is strongly recommended. Sessions should be capped at 20–25 minutes in Zone 2.

### Walking (Outdoor or Treadmill): Zone 1 Foundation

Brisk walking is underrated as a cardiovascular tool for perimenopausal women. It is weight-bearing (providing a modest bone loading stimulus), low thermoregulatory stress at Zone 1 intensity, and has the lowest barrier to adherence of any modality. Walking outdoors in the morning — before ambient temperatures peak — is a practical and evidence-supported habit for this client.

**Outdoor walking in summer:** Schedule before 9:00 am or after 18:00 pm to avoid peak heat. Carry cold water. Wear light, breathable clothing. A cooling neck wrap is a practical accessory for outdoor summer walking.

**Treadmill walking** in an air-conditioned gym is the thermally safest option and allows precise speed and incline control. An incline of 4–8% at 5–6 km/h provides a meaningful cardiovascular stimulus while keeping heart rate firmly in Zone 1.

### Running: Conditional Inclusion

Running is not excluded from this programme, but it carries the highest thermoregulatory load of the common cardio modalities due to the combination of large muscle mass engagement, upright posture, and the absence of passive cooling. For a client with significant heat intolerance, running in warm weather is high risk for vasomotor symptom precipitation.

Running is therefore included only under the following conditions:
- Treadmill in an air-conditioned environment, or outdoor running before 8:00 am or after 19:00 pm during June–August
- Zone 1 to lower Zone 2 intensity only (below 125 bpm) for steady-state runs
- Sessions capped at 30 minutes
- Cold water available throughout
- Never on the same day as a lower body resistance session

If your client is an experienced runner who values it highly, these conditions allow her to maintain the habit safely. If running is not a priority for her, the other modalities above are preferable choices for this programme.

## Before Adjusting the Dial: A Clinical Checkpoint

Pushing intensity in Phase 2 for this client is appropriate and achievable. She is an advanced lifter with an established fitness base, and progressive overload — in both resistance and cardiovascular training — is the correct direction of travel. However, intensifying Phase 2 for a perimenopausal woman with significant vasomotor symptoms during the hottest month of the year requires more than simply adding load and shortening rest periods. It requires a deliberate recalibration of every variable that interacts with intensity: recovery, nutrition timing, cooling infrastructure, readiness thresholds, and session sequencing.

The following revised Phase 2 is genuinely harder than the original. It is also more carefully managed. These two things are not in tension — they are the same thing done properly.

**Three non-negotiables before any elevated-intensity session proceeds:**

First, your client must have eaten a pre-session meal containing at least 25 g of protein and 30 g of carbohydrate within 60–90 minutes of training. Fasted high-intensity work is explicitly contraindicated for this client, and at the intensities prescribed below, the performance and safety case for pre-session fuelling is even stronger than in Phase 1.

Second, the training environment must be actively cooled. Air conditioning or a powerful fan directed at the training space is not optional at these intensities. If the gym temperature exceeds 20°C, reduce all working loads by 10% and cap cardio intervals at Phase 1 parameters. This is a standing instruction for the entire phase, not a session-by-session judgement call.

Third, readiness scores must be 17 or above for elevated-intensity resistance work and 19 or above for Zone 3 cardio intervals. Below these thresholds, the session defaults to the Phase 1 parameters. This is not a soft option — it is the mechanism by which the programme remains sustainable across eight weeks of progressive loading.

## Revised Phase 2 Resistance Programming

### Intensity and Loading Parameters

The original Phase 2 prescribed 75–85% of 1RM for main lifts. The revised Phase 2 pushes this to **80–90% of 1RM**, with the following structural changes:

**Rep ranges decrease as intensity increases.** At 88–90% 1RM, sets of 3 are appropriate. At 80–83%, sets of 4–5 remain viable. The programme uses a wave-loading structure across the four weeks rather than simple linear progression, which allows intensity to peak in Week 7 without accumulating excessive fatigue across the entire phase.

**Wave loading structure:**
- Week 5: 82% 1RM — moderate-high intensity, higher volume
- Week 6: 87% 1RM — high intensity, moderate volume
- Week 7: 90% 1RM — peak intensity, lower volume
- Week 8: Deload — 65% 1RM, full recovery

This wave pattern means your client reaches a genuine near-maximal effort in Week 7 without the connective tissue and nervous system fatigue that would accumulate from four consecutive weeks of linear loading at high intensity. The descent into Week 8 deload is therefore from a true peak rather than from accumulated exhaustion.

**Contrast training is retained and progressed.** The explosive component of Thursday and Friday sessions becomes more demanding in Phase 2 revised, with heavier contrast loads and more complex explosive movements.

**Rest periods increase at higher intensities.** At 88–90% 1RM, the nervous system requires more recovery between sets than at 75–80%. Rest periods for main compound lifts extend to 3.5–4 minutes in Weeks 6 and 7. This is not inefficiency — it is the physiological requirement for expressing near-maximal strength safely and repeatedly.

### Week 5 (29 June – 5 July 2026)
**Loading: 82% 1RM | Volume: High | Character: Strength-Volume**

The first week of Phase 2 revised uses a higher volume approach at the lower end of the intensity range. This serves as a bridge from Phase 1 and prepares the neuromuscular system for the heavier loads in Weeks 6 and 7. Your client should finish Week 5 sessions feeling that she worked hard but could have done more — this is intentional.

**Monday — Lower Body Strength**

Warm-up: 5 minutes easy cycling in cool environment, hip 90/90 mobility, glute bridges × 15, banded clamshells × 15 each side. Three warm-up sets of back squat: 40% × 5, 60% × 3, 72% × 2 (the final warm-up set is closer to working weight than in Phase 1, preparing the nervous system more specifically).

*Main work:*

**Back Squat: 5 sets × 4 reps at 82% 1RM. Rest 3.5 minutes.**

The rep count is 4 rather than 5 at this intensity. Each set should feel like an RPE of 7.5–8 — hard, requiring genuine focus, but with one to two reps clearly remaining. If any set reaches RPE 9 or above, reduce the load by 2.5 kg for subsequent sets. Bar speed is the key quality indicator: if the concentric phase slows dramatically on the third or fourth rep, the load is appropriate. If it slows on the second rep, reduce load. Maintain the 3-second eccentric from Phase 1 — do not sacrifice eccentric control for heavier loading.

**Pause Squat: 3 sets × 3 reps at 70% 1RM. Rest 3 minutes.**

This is a new exercise introduced in Phase 2 revised. The pause squat — a 3-second pause at the bottom of the squat before driving upward — eliminates the stretch-shortening cycle contribution and forces the muscles to generate force from a dead stop. It is significantly harder than a regular squat at the same load, which is why the percentage is lower. The pause squat has strong evidence for improving positional strength at the bottom of the squat, which transfers directly to heavier back squat performance. It also places a sustained compressive load on the femoral neck and lumbar vertebrae, making it an excellent bone density stimulus.

**Romanian Deadlift: 4 sets × 5 reps at 78% 1RM. Rest 3 minutes.**

Increase from Phase 1 loading. The eccentric phase remains controlled at 3–4 seconds. At this load, your client should feel a strong hamstring stretch at the bottom of each rep. If lumbar rounding occurs at any point, reduce load — spinal position is non-negotiable.

**Bulgarian Split Squat: 3 sets × 6 reps each leg, with heavy dumbbells. Rest 2.5 minutes.**

Heavier than Phase 1. The load should be challenging enough that the final two reps of each set require genuine effort. If your client has been using 16–18 kg dumbbells in Phase 1, target 20–22 kg in Week 5.

**Farmer's Carry: 3 sets × 40 metres, heavy. Rest 2 minutes.**

Progressed from Phase 1 in both load and distance. The carry should be heavy enough that grip and core stability are genuinely challenged by the 30-metre mark. Upright posture throughout — no lateral lean.

**Copenhagen Plank: 3 sets × 20 seconds each side. Rest 90 seconds.**

A new addition in Phase 2 revised. The Copenhagen plank is a side plank variation with the top leg supported on a bench, creating a significant adductor and lateral core demand. It is one of the most effective exercises for hip adductor strength, which is directly relevant to knee stability under heavy squat loads and to bone loading at the femoral neck. Begin with the easier variation (bottom knee on the floor) if needed and progress to the full variation (bottom leg unsupported) as strength allows.

**Tuesday — Upper Body Strength**

Warm-up: band pull-aparts × 25, shoulder CARs × 5 each direction, face pulls × 20 with light resistance, two warm-up sets of bench press at 45% and 65%.

*Main work:*

**Barbell Bench Press: 5 sets × 4 reps at 82% 1RM. Rest 3.5 minutes.**

Same loading logic as the back squat. RPE 7.5–8 per set. Controlled 3-second descent, brief pause on the chest (not a bounce), explosive drive upward. The explosive intent on the concentric phase is important even at this load — attempting to move the bar as fast as possible, even when it moves slowly due to the weight, recruits more motor units and produces greater strength adaptation than a slow, grinding concentric.

**Close-Grip Bench Press: 3 sets × 5 reps at 72% 1RM. Rest 2.5 minutes.**

New exercise in Phase 2 revised. The close-grip variation shifts emphasis to the triceps and medial pectoral fibres, addressing a different portion of the pressing musculature than the standard grip. It also reduces shoulder joint stress compared to a wide grip, making it a useful variation for long-term shoulder health. Grip width should be approximately shoulder-width — not excessively narrow, which increases wrist stress.

**Barbell Bent-Over Row: 5 sets × 4 reps at 80% 1RM. Rest 3 minutes.**

Significant load increase from Phase 1. At this intensity, the row becomes a genuine strength exercise rather than a volume exercise. Maintain a rigid torso — no hip drive or body English to complete the rep. If form breaks down, the load is too heavy.

**Weighted Pull-Up or Lat Pulldown: 4 sets × 4–5 reps. Rest 2.5 minutes.**

If your client can perform pull-ups, add load via a dipping belt or weighted vest. Target a load that makes 4–5 reps genuinely challenging. If using lat pulldown, increase load significantly from Phase 1 — this should be a strength set, not a hypertrophy set.

**Seated Dumbbell Overhead Press: 3 sets × 5 reps, heavy. Rest 2.5 minutes.**

Heavier than Phase 1. The seated position is maintained to protect the lumbar spine under heavier loads.

**Face Pull: 4 sets × 15 reps. Rest 90 seconds.**

Volume increases from Phase 1. Load remains moderate — this is a shoulder health exercise and should never be loaded to the point where form degrades. The additional set reflects the increased pressing volume in Phase 2 revised and the need to maintain rotator cuff balance.

**Tricep Pushdown: 3 sets × 8 reps, heavy. Rest 90 seconds.**

**Thursday — Lower Body Power/Hypertrophy with Advanced Contrast**

The contrast training in Phase 2 revised is progressed in two ways: the heavy component uses higher loads, and the explosive component uses more demanding movements that require greater power output and coordination.

Warm-up: same as Monday plus 5 broad jumps at 50% effort to prime the nervous system for explosive work.

*Main work:*

**Trap Bar Deadlift + Depth Drop to Broad Jump: 5 sets. Rest 4 minutes between pairs.**

Heavy component: 4 reps at 85% 1RM. Rest 15 seconds, then immediately perform the explosive component.

Explosive component: 3 Depth Drop to Broad Jumps. Set up a small box or step (20–30 cm). Step off (do not jump off) the box, land on both feet, immediately absorb the landing and redirect into a maximal broad jump forward. Land softly, reset, repeat. The depth drop creates a rapid eccentric loading stimulus that potentiates the nervous system for the subsequent jump — this is a more advanced contrast pairing than the simple broad jump used in the original Phase 2.

**Important safety note:** The depth drop to broad jump is a plyometric exercise with a meaningful impact load. Ensure your client has demonstrated good landing mechanics (soft knees, hip hinge on landing, no knee valgus) before progressing to this variation. If landing mechanics are poor, revert to the standard broad jump from Phase 1.

**Leg Press: 4 sets × 6 reps, heavy. Rest 2.5 minutes.**

Higher foot placement to emphasise glutes and hamstrings. Load should be significantly heavier than Phase 1 — this is a strength set.

**Rear-Foot Elevated Split Squat (Barbell): 3 sets × 5 reps each leg. Rest 2.5 minutes.**

Progression from the dumbbell Bulgarian split squat. Moving the load to a barbell across the upper back increases the stability demand and allows heavier loading. This is a technically demanding exercise — ensure your client is comfortable with the movement pattern before adding significant load.

**Nordic Hamstring Curl: 4 sets × 5 reps with 3-second eccentric. Rest 2.5 minutes.**

The addition of a controlled 3-second eccentric phase significantly increases the difficulty and the hamstring tendon loading stimulus. This is one of the most effective exercises for hamstring injury prevention and is particularly relevant for perimenopausal women given the increased tendon injury risk associated with declining oestrogen.

**Suitcase Carry: 3 sets × 25 metres each side, heavy. Rest 2 minutes.**

Progressed from Phase 1 in both load and distance.

# Hot Yoga: Clinical Assessment & Alternative Recommendation

**Regarding the Proposed Addition to the 12-Week Programme**

---

## Direct Answer First

Do not add hot yoga to this programme. Not in Phase 1, not in Phase 2, not in Phase 3, and not as an occasional supplement to the existing sessions. For this specific client, at this specific point in her health history, hot yoga is contraindicated. This is not a conservative or overly cautious position — it follows directly from the clinical picture you have already described and from the physiological mechanisms that underpin her vasomotor symptoms.

This document explains that position in full, so you can have an informed conversation with your client rather than simply telling her no. It then presents a structured flexibility and mobility programme that will deliver everything she is hoping to get from hot yoga — and in several respects more — without the risks that hot yoga carries for her.

---

## Why Hot Yoga Is Contraindicated for This Client

### The Thermoregulatory Problem Is Fundamental, Not Incidental

Your client's vasomotor symptoms — the hot flashes and heat intolerance — are not a minor inconvenience that can be managed around. They are the surface expression of a fundamental dysregulation in hypothalamic thermoregulation. To understand why hot yoga is specifically problematic, it helps to understand this mechanism precisely.

In a hormonally stable woman, the hypothalamus maintains core temperature within a thermoneutral zone — a range of approximately 0.4°C within which neither sweating nor shivering is triggered. Fluctuating and declining oestrogen narrows this thermoneutral zone dramatically, sometimes to near zero. This means that very small increases in core temperature — increases that a younger woman's hypothalamus would not even register — are sufficient to trigger the full vasomotor response: peripheral vasodilation, profuse sweating, and the subjective experience of a hot flash.

Hot yoga is conducted in a room heated to 35–42°C with humidity levels of 40–60%. This environment is specifically designed to raise core temperature rapidly and substantially. For a woman with a narrowed thermoneutral zone, entering a hot yoga studio is not a mild thermal challenge — it is a direct and sustained assault on the very regulatory system that is already failing her. The result is not that she will have a hot flash during class. The result is that she will almost certainly have multiple severe hot flashes during class, that her core temperature will rise to levels that impair cognitive function and physical performance, and that the physiological stress of the session will likely worsen her vasomotor symptoms for hours or days afterward through the cortisol and inflammatory pathways that heat stress activates.

This is not speculation. The relationship between environmental heat exposure and vasomotor symptom precipitation and worsening in perimenopausal women is well-established. The GP restriction on sauna use reflects exactly this understanding. Hot yoga and sauna are physiologically equivalent in the relevant respect: both involve sustained exposure to a hot environment that raises core temperature well above the threshold at which your client's hypothalamus triggers a vasomotor response.

### The Specific Risks in a Hot Yoga Environment

Beyond the vasomotor symptom precipitation, hot yoga carries several additional risks for this client that are worth articulating clearly.

**Dehydration and electrolyte loss.** Hot yoga produces significant sweat losses — studies have measured sweat rates of 1–2 litres per hour in heated yoga environments. Your client already has elevated fluid loss from vasomotor sweating. The combination of exercise-induced sweating and vasomotor sweating in a hot environment creates a dehydration risk that is substantially higher than for a younger woman without vasomotor symptoms. Dehydration impairs thermoregulation further, creating a negative feedback loop: the hotter she gets, the more she sweats, the more dehydrated she becomes, the less effectively her body can cool itself, the hotter she gets.

**Hypermobility risk under heat.** This is a less commonly discussed but clinically important concern. Heat increases tissue extensibility — muscles and connective tissues become more pliable at elevated temperatures. In a yoga context, this means that the range of motion achievable in a hot room is significantly greater than the range achievable at normal temperature. For a younger woman with healthy connective tissue, this is the point — it allows deeper stretching. For a perimenopausal woman whose oestrogen decline is already reducing collagen synthesis and altering tendon and ligament mechanical properties, the combination of thermally increased tissue extensibility and the sustained end-range loading of yoga poses creates a meaningful risk of connective tissue overstretching and injury. She may achieve ranges of motion in a hot yoga class that her connective tissue cannot safely sustain, and she may not feel the warning signals that would normally prevent her from going too far because the heat blunts proprioceptive feedback.

**Cardiovascular stress.** Hot environments significantly increase cardiovascular demand. Heart rate at a given exercise intensity is substantially higher in heat than in thermoneutral conditions, and cardiac output must increase to support both the exercising muscles and the peripheral vasodilation required for heat dissipation. For a perimenopausal woman, whose cardiovascular risk profile is beginning to shift with declining oestrogen, adding unnecessary cardiovascular stress through environmental heat is not a neutral choice.

**Interaction with the resistance programme.** Your client is training four days per week at progressively high intensities. Recovery is already the limiting factor in her programme. Hot yoga sessions would add significant physiological stress — not just the mechanical stress of the yoga itself, but the thermoregulatory, cardiovascular, and hormonal stress of the heated environment — on days that are currently designated for recovery. This would compromise her resistance training performance and increase her injury risk across the entire programme.

### Addressing the Flexibility Belief Directly

Your client has heard that hot yoga helps with flexibility. This is partially true but requires unpacking, because the mechanism matters enormously for her situation.

Hot yoga improves acute flexibility — the range of motion achievable during and immediately after a session — primarily through the thermal effect on tissue extensibility described above. This is a transient effect. When core temperature returns to normal, tissue extensibility returns to baseline. The long-term flexibility improvements attributed to regular hot yoga practice are largely the result of the yoga itself — the consistent stretching, the neuromuscular adaptations, the improved motor control and body awareness — not the heat. The heat is a delivery mechanism that makes the stretching feel easier and allows greater range of motion in the short term, but it is not the active ingredient for lasting flexibility change.

This means that a well-designed flexibility and mobility programme conducted at normal temperature will produce equivalent or superior long-term flexibility outcomes compared to hot yoga, without any of the thermoregulatory risks. The yoga without the hot room is not a compromise — it is the better intervention for this client.

---

## What She Actually Needs: A Comprehensive Flexibility & Mobility Programme

The following programme is designed to deliver the flexibility, mobility, stress reduction, and body awareness benefits your client is seeking from hot yoga, integrated into the existing 12-week structure. It draws on yoga, dynamic mobility work, and targeted static stretching, all conducted in a thermally safe environment.

### Distinguishing Flexibility from Mobility

Before presenting the programme, it is worth clarifying the distinction between flexibility and mobility, because they require different training approaches and your client likely needs both.

**Flexibility** is the passive range of motion available at a joint — how far a muscle can be lengthened when an external force (gravity, a strap, a partner) is applied. It is a property of the muscle and connective tissue.

**Mobility** is the active range of motion available at a joint — how far you can move through a range under your own muscular control. It is a property of the neuromuscular system as much as the connective tissue. Mobility is what actually matters for athletic performance, injury prevention, and functional movement quality.

A woman can be highly flexible — able to achieve large ranges of motion passively — but have poor mobility if she cannot actively control those ranges. Conversely, a woman with moderate flexibility but excellent mobility will move better, lift more safely, and be less injury-prone than a highly flexible woman with poor motor control.

Your client needs both, but mobility is the higher priority given her resistance training programme. The programme below addresses both systematically.

## Tuesday and Friday Evening Flexibility Extensions (20 Minutes)

These sessions follow immediately after the resistance training session, before your client showers or changes. The muscles are warm, the nervous system is in a post-exercise state that is receptive to stretching, and the parasympathetic shift of slow, deliberate stretching will support recovery.

The sequence is the same on both Tuesday and Friday, with minor variations noted. All stretches are held for 60–90 seconds — longer than the 30-second holds commonly recommended, because research consistently shows that 60–90 second holds produce greater lasting flexibility change than shorter holds, particularly in adults over 40.

**The environment matters.** These sessions should be conducted in the cool-down area of the gym or in a cool room. A fan is appropriate. Cold water should be available. If your client feels a hot flash beginning during this session, she pauses, applies a cooling towel, sips cold water, and resumes when comfortable. The slow, parasympathetic nature of stretching makes hot flash precipitation less likely than during cardio, but it can still occur.

**Tuesday Evening Extension — Lower Body and Hip Focus**

*Following upper body resistance training, the lower body has not been heavily loaded today. This makes Tuesday evening an ideal time for deeper lower body flexibility work.*

**Supine Hip Flexor Stretch (Figure-4 variation): 90 seconds each side.**
Lying on the back, cross one ankle over the opposite knee, flex the hip to bring both legs toward the chest. This targets the piriformis and deep hip external rotators — muscles that become chronically shortened in women who sit for extended periods and that directly affect squat depth and hip mobility. The supine position is preferable to the standing figure-4 for this client as it removes balance demands and allows complete muscular relaxation.

**Half-Kneeling Hip Flexor Stretch with Reach: 90 seconds each side.**
In a half-kneeling position (one knee on the floor, one foot forward), posteriorly tilt the pelvis and drive the hips forward until a stretch is felt in the front of the rear hip. Add an ipsilateral reach overhead to increase the stretch through the thoracolumbar fascia and lateral hip flexors. The hip flexors — particularly the iliopsoas — are chronically shortened in most adults and directly limit squat depth, hip extension in the deadlift, and running mechanics.

**Supine Hamstring Stretch with Strap: 90 seconds each side.**
Lying on the back, loop a yoga strap or resistance band around one foot and extend the leg toward the ceiling. Keep the opposite leg flat on the floor. This is a more effective hamstring stretch than the standing toe-touch because it isolates the hamstring without the confounding effect of lumbar flexion. At 90 seconds, the nervous system's protective tension response (the stretch reflex) begins to subside and genuine tissue lengthening can occur.

**Seated Adductor Stretch (Butterfly): 90 seconds.**
Seated on the floor, soles of the feet together, knees falling outward. Lean forward from the hips — not the lumbar spine — to increase the stretch. The adductors are frequently neglected in flexibility work but are directly relevant to squat mechanics and hip health. The Copenhagen plank in the resistance programme loads the adductors; this stretch addresses their flexibility.

**90/90 Hip Stretch: 90 seconds each side.**
Seated on the floor with both hips at 90 degrees — front leg externally rotated, rear leg internally rotated. This position simultaneously stretches the external rotators of the front hip and the internal rotators and hip flexors of the rear hip. It is one of the most comprehensive single hip stretches available and directly addresses the hip mobility demands of the squat and deadlift patterns.

**Supine Spinal Twist: 60 seconds each side.**
Lying on the back, draw one knee to the chest and guide it across the body with the opposite hand, allowing the spine to rotate. Keep both shoulders on the floor. This addresses thoracic and lumbar rotation, which is often restricted in lifters who train primarily in the sagittal plane.

**Child's Pose with Lateral Reach: 60 seconds each side.**
From a kneeling position, sit back toward the heels and extend the arms forward on the floor. Walk the hands to one side to create a lateral stretch through the latissimus dorsi and quadratus lumborum. These muscles are heavily loaded in the resistance programme and benefit from deliberate lengthening.

**Legs Up the Wall (Viparita Karani): 3 minutes.**
Lie on the back with the legs extended up a wall, hips as close to the wall as comfortable. This is a restorative yoga pose with a specific physiological benefit: the passive inversion promotes venous return from the lower limbs, reduces lower leg swelling, and activates the parasympathetic nervous system. It is also one of the most effective positions for reducing hot flash frequency in the immediate post-exercise period, as the supine position and leg elevation reduce the cardiovascular demand and support core temperature normalisation. End every Tuesday and Friday flexibility session with this pose.

**Friday Evening Extension — Upper Body and Thoracic Focus**

*Following upper body resistance training, the upper body musculature is warm and the thoracic spine has been loaded. Friday's flexibility extension therefore emphasises upper body and thoracic mobility.*

**Doorway Chest Stretch: 90 seconds, three arm positions.**
Stand in a doorway with one forearm against the frame. Gently rotate the body away from the arm to stretch the pectoral muscles and anterior shoulder. Perform at three arm heights: low (hand at hip height, targeting lower pectorals), middle (elbow at shoulder height, targeting mid pectorals and anterior deltoid), and high (elbow above shoulder height, targeting upper pectorals and bicipital tendon). Heavy pressing volume in the resistance programme creates chronic shortening of the anterior chest — this stretch directly counteracts that.

**Thread the Needle: 60 seconds each side.**
From a quadruped position (hands and knees), slide one arm under the body along the floor, allowing the thoracic spine to rotate. This is one of the most effective thoracic rotation stretches available and directly addresses the thoracic mobility demands of the overhead press and row patterns.

**Thoracic Extension over Foam Roller: 60 seconds at three spinal levels.**
Place a foam roller perpendicular to the spine at the mid-thoracic level. Support the head with the hands and gently extend over the roller. Move the roller to three positions: lower thoracic (approximately T10), mid-thoracic (T7), and upper thoracic (T4). This addresses the thoracic kyphosis that develops with heavy anterior loading and directly improves overhead press mechanics and scapular positioning.

**Lat Stretch with Dowel or Strap: 90 seconds each side.**
Hold a dowel or strap overhead with both hands, then allow one side to drop while the other arm reaches overhead and slightly across the body. The latissimus dorsi is the primary muscle limiting overhead shoulder mobility in most lifters, and its chronic shortening from pull-ups, rows, and deadlifts directly restricts the overhead press range of motion.

**Sleeper Stretch: 60 seconds each side.**
Lying on one side with the shoulder at 90 degrees of abduction and the elbow at 90 degrees of flexion, use the opposite hand to gently press the forearm toward the floor. This stretches the posterior shoulder capsule and infraspinatus — structures that become tight with heavy pressing volume and that, when restricted, contribute to shoulder impingement and rotator cuff pathology.

Seated, gently tilt the ear toward the shoulder and apply light overpressure with the same-side hand. The upper trapezius and levator scapulae are chronically overloaded in women who carry stress tension in the neck and shoulders, and their tightness directly affects scapular mechanics during pressing and pulling movements.

**Supine Thoracic Rotation Stretch: 60 seconds each side.**
Lying on the side with hips stacked and knees bent at 90 degrees, extend both arms forward at shoulder height. Keep the lower arm on the floor and rotate the upper arm open toward the ceiling, following with the eyes and allowing the thoracic spine to rotate. Hold at end range.

This is the centrepiece of the flexibility programme — the session that most closely approximates what your client was hoping to get from hot yoga, conducted safely and with greater specificity to her needs.

The session is structured in four parts: a dynamic mobility warm-up, a strength-through-range block, a yoga flow sequence, and a restorative close. The progression from dynamic to static, and from active to passive, mirrors the structure of a well-designed yoga class and produces the same parasympathetic shift and body awareness development that your client is seeking.

**Environment:** Cool room, ideally air-conditioned. Fan available. Cold water present. Yoga mat, two yoga blocks, a strap, and a bolster or firm pillow. Wear light, breathable clothing. The room temperature should be comfortable — not cold, but not warm. 18–21°C is ideal.
