### Part 1: Dynamic Mobility Warm-Up (10 minutes)

Dynamic mobility work — moving through ranges of motion under active muscular control — is the foundation of the session. It raises tissue temperature gently, activates the neuromuscular system, and prepares the joints for the deeper work to follow. Unlike static stretching, dynamic mobility work improves both flexibility and mobility simultaneously.

**Cat-Cow: 10 slow repetitions.**
On hands and knees, alternate between spinal flexion (cat) and spinal extension (cow). Move slowly and deliberately, segmenting the spine — initiate the movement from the tailbone and let it travel vertebra by vertebra to the neck. This is a fundamental spinal mobility exercise that directly addresses the segmental stiffness that develops from heavy lifting.

**World's Greatest Stretch: 5 repetitions each side.**
From a standing position, step forward into a deep lunge. Place the same-side hand on the floor inside the front foot. Rotate the opposite arm toward the ceiling, following with the eyes. Return to standing and repeat on the other side. This single movement addresses hip flexor length, thoracic rotation, ankle dorsiflexion, and hamstring flexibility simultaneously — it is arguably the most efficient single mobility exercise available.

**Hip Circle (Controlled Articular Rotation): 10 circles each direction each hip.**
Standing on one leg, draw the opposite knee up and make large, slow circles with the hip joint — forward, out, back, in. This is a controlled articular rotation (CAR) that takes the hip through its full available range under active muscular control. CARs are the most direct method of improving joint mobility (as distinct from flexibility) and are particularly important for hip health in a woman doing heavy squats and deadlifts.

**Shoulder CAR: 5 circles each direction each shoulder.**
Standing with the arm at the side, make the largest possible circle with the shoulder joint — forward, up, back, down — keeping the rest of the body completely still. This is the shoulder equivalent of the hip CAR and directly addresses the shoulder mobility demands of the overhead press and pull-up patterns.

**Thoracic Rotation in Quadruped: 10 repetitions each side.**
On hands and knees, place one hand behind the head. Rotate the elbow toward the opposite hand, then open it toward the ceiling. Move slowly and breathe into the rotation. This is a more active version of the thread-the-needle stretch from the evening sessions.

**Ankle Circles and Dorsiflexion Mobilisation: 10 circles each direction, then 10 wall ankle mobilisations each side.**
Ankle dorsiflexion is frequently the limiting factor in squat depth. The wall ankle mobilisation — standing close to a wall, driving the knee forward over the toes while keeping the heel on the floor — directly addresses this restriction.

**Inchworm with Push-Up: 5 repetitions.**
From standing, hinge forward and walk the hands out to a plank position. Perform one push-up. Walk the hands back and stand. This integrates hamstring flexibility, shoulder stability, and spinal control in a single flowing movement.

---

### Part 2: Strength Through Range (15 minutes)

This block is the element most absent from conventional yoga and most important for your client's long-term joint health. Strength through range — developing muscular strength at end ranges of motion, not just in the mid-range where most resistance training occurs — is what converts passive flexibility into functional mobility and what protects joints from injury at extreme ranges.

**Deep Squat Hold with Heel Elevation (if needed): 3 × 60 seconds.**
Hold the bottom of a squat for 60 seconds, using a doorframe or TRX for support if needed. Focus on keeping the chest up, the knees tracking over the toes, and the weight distributed evenly across the foot. This develops the positional strength and tissue tolerance at the bottom of the squat that directly transfers to back squat performance. Lying on the back with one leg extended toward the ceiling, actively lower the leg toward the floor as slowly as possible while keeping it straight, then use the hands to return it to the start position. This develops eccentric hamstring strength through the full range of hip flexion — the same range that is loaded in the Romanian deadlift and Nordic hamstring curl. It is a safer and more controlled introduction to end-range hamstring loading than the Nordic curl itself.

**Cossack Squat: 3 × 6 repetitions each side.**
Standing with feet wide, shift the weight to one side and lower into a deep lateral lunge, keeping the opposite leg straight with the foot flat or toes raised. This develops hip adductor strength and flexibility, inner thigh mobility, and ankle dorsiflexion simultaneously. It is one of the most comprehensive lower body mobility exercises available and directly addresses the lateral hip and adductor restrictions that limit squat depth and hip health.

**Prone Hip Extension (Glute Activation at End Range): 3 × 10 repetitions each side.**
Lying face down, bend one knee to 90 degrees and lift the thigh off the floor by squeezing the glute. Hold for 2 seconds at the top. This develops glute strength at the end range of hip extension — the range that is most important for the top of the deadlift and the drive phase of the squat, and the range where most women are weakest.

Standing with the back against a wall, feet slightly forward, arms bent at 90 degrees with the backs of the hands against the wall. Slide the arms upward while maintaining contact between the hands, elbows, and wall throughout. This develops lower trapezius strength and thoracic extension mobility simultaneously — the combination that is most important for overhead pressing mechanics and scapular health.

**Regarding the Proposed Addition to the 12-Week Programme**

---

## Direct Answer First

No. Fasted morning HIIT cannot be added to this programme for this client. This is not a matter of preference, caution, or conservative programming philosophy. It is a direct clinical contraindication that was established by the client's GP and documented in the original programme brief. The restriction reads explicitly: **no fasted HIIT in heat**. The summer timing of this programme — June through August — means that morning sessions occur during the warmest part of the year, compounding the contraindication further.

Adding fasted morning HIIT to this programme would require overriding a GP instruction. That is outside the scope of personal training practice, and it would expose both your client and you to meaningful risk.

This document explains precisely why the contraindication exists, addresses the fat loss goal directly with evidence-based alternatives, and gives you the language to have this conversation with your client in a way that is honest, respectful, and clinically grounded.

---

## Why This Specific Combination Is Contraindicated

The restriction is not on HIIT alone. It is not on fasted training alone. It is not on morning training alone. It is on the specific combination of all three, and understanding why that combination is uniquely problematic for this client requires looking at each component and then at how they interact.

### Fasted Training in Perimenopause

Training in a fasted state — typically defined as more than 8 hours since the last meal, which morning training almost always satisfies — produces a specific hormonal environment. Cortisol is at its natural diurnal peak in the early morning, a phenomenon called the cortisol awakening response. This morning cortisol peak serves a legitimate physiological purpose: it mobilises energy substrates, raises alertness, and prepares the body for the demands of the day. In a hormonally stable younger woman, this cortisol peak is well-regulated and returns to baseline within a couple of hours.

In perimenopause, the picture is different. Fluctuating oestrogen and progesterone directly affect the sensitivity and regulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis — the system that controls cortisol production. The result is that perimenopausal women frequently have dysregulated cortisol patterns: higher morning peaks, slower return to baseline, and greater cortisol reactivity to stressors including exercise. Adding a training session to the already-elevated morning cortisol peak, in a fasted state that removes the buffering effect of food on the stress response, produces a cortisol spike that is substantially larger than the same session performed fed later in the day.

The consequences of this cortisol spike are directly counterproductive to the fat loss goal your client is pursuing. Chronically elevated cortisol promotes fat storage, specifically visceral abdominal fat — the fat that perimenopausal women are already predisposed to accumulate due to declining oestrogen. It also promotes muscle protein breakdown, which is the opposite of what an advanced lifter needs. It impairs sleep quality, which further dysregulates appetite hormones and worsens body composition. And it worsens vasomotor symptoms, because cortisol and the inflammatory pathways it activates interact directly with the hypothalamic thermoregulatory dysfunction that underlies hot flashes.

Fasted training for fat loss is a strategy that has a reasonable evidence base in younger, hormonally stable populations. In perimenopausal women with significant vasomotor symptoms, it is likely to worsen the hormonal environment in ways that actively impede fat loss and harm overall health.

### HIIT and the Vasomotor Response

High-intensity interval training produces the most rapid and substantial core temperature rise of any common exercise modality. The combination of large muscle mass recruitment, high metabolic rate, and the repeated sprint-recovery pattern of HIIT means that core temperature can rise by 1.5–2°C within the first few minutes of a genuine HIIT session. For a woman with a narrowed thermoneutral zone, this is sufficient to trigger severe vasomotor responses almost immediately.

The problem is not just the discomfort of hot flashes during the session. The problem is the physiological cascade that follows. A severe vasomotor response during high-intensity exercise involves simultaneous peripheral vasodilation — blood being redirected to the skin for cooling — and the high cardiac output demands of the exercise itself. These two demands compete directly. The cardiovascular system cannot simultaneously maximise blood flow to working muscles for exercise performance and maximise blood flow to the skin for thermoregulation. The result is compromised performance, elevated heart rate beyond what the exercise intensity alone would produce, and a significantly increased cardiovascular stress that is inappropriate for a client whose cardiovascular risk profile is already shifting with perimenopause.

Beyond the session itself, HIIT produces a substantial post-exercise cortisol elevation that persists for several hours. In a fed state, later in the day, in a cool environment, this cortisol response is manageable. In a fasted state, in the morning, when cortisol is already at its diurnal peak, the combined cortisol load is very high. For this client, that means worsened vasomotor symptoms for the remainder of the day, impaired recovery from the resistance training sessions that are the foundation of her programme, and the chronic cortisol-driven fat storage effect described above.

### The Heat Component

The programme runs from June through August. In the Northern Hemisphere, morning temperatures during this period are not the cool refuge they might be in other seasons. By 7:00 am in July, ambient temperatures in many UK and European locations are already 18–22°C and rising. Humidity is often elevated in the morning hours. If your client is training outdoors — which morning HIIT often implies — she is doing so in an environment that is already thermally challenging for a woman with heat intolerance, before the exercise-generated heat load is added.

Even indoor morning HIIT carries this risk if the gym has not been cooled overnight. Many gyms are warmer in the morning than later in the day, before air conditioning has had time to bring the space to a comfortable temperature.

The GP restriction specifically names heat as a component of the contraindication. This is not incidental. It reflects a clinical understanding that the combination of fasted state, high-intensity exercise, and warm environment creates a thermoregulatory and hormonal stress that is qualitatively different from any one of these factors alone.

---

## Addressing the Fat Loss Goal Directly

Your client wants to lose fat. This is a legitimate goal and one that the programme can support effectively. But it is important to be honest with her about the evidence base for fasted HIIT as a fat loss strategy, because the belief that it is uniquely effective is widespread and largely incorrect.

### The Fasted HIIT Fat Loss Myth

The theoretical basis for fasted HIIT as a fat loss tool is that exercising in a fasted state, when glycogen stores are lower and insulin levels are minimal, forces the body to rely more heavily on fat oxidation for fuel. This is true in a narrow biochemical sense — fat oxidation is indeed higher during fasted exercise than fed exercise at the same intensity.

However, the relevant question for fat loss is not what fuel is burned during the exercise session. It is what happens to total fat balance over 24 hours, 48 hours, and weeks. When this question is asked, the fasted HIIT advantage disappears. Multiple well-controlled studies comparing fasted and fed exercise for fat loss, when total caloric intake is matched, show no significant difference in fat loss outcomes between the two conditions. The body compensates for the increased fat oxidation during fasted exercise by reducing fat oxidation at other times of day, and by increasing appetite in ways that often lead to greater caloric intake in the hours following fasted training.

For this specific client, the calculation is even less favourable. The cortisol-driven muscle breakdown that fasted HIIT produces means that some of the weight lost through this approach would be lean mass rather than fat — the opposite of what an advanced lifter needs. And the cortisol-driven visceral fat storage that follows repeated fasted HIIT sessions in a perimenopausal woman may actually increase abdominal fat deposition over time, despite the caloric expenditure of the sessions.

The fat loss goal is real and valid. Fasted morning HIIT is simply not an effective or safe tool for achieving it in this client's context.

### What Actually Works for Fat Loss in Perimenopause

The evidence base for fat loss in perimenopausal women points consistently toward a different set of interventions than those that work in younger populations. The following are the most effective levers available, all of which are already present or can be added to this programme without clinical risk.

**Progressive resistance training is the primary fat loss tool.** This may seem counterintuitive, but the evidence is clear. Resistance training builds and preserves lean muscle mass, which is the primary determinant of resting metabolic rate. In perimenopause, when muscle mass is under threat from declining anabolic hormones, maintaining and building muscle through resistance training is the most powerful intervention available for long-term body composition improvement. Your client is already doing this. The 12-week programme is, in this sense, already a fat loss programme — it is simply working through the mechanism of metabolic rate preservation rather than acute caloric expenditure.

**Zone 2 cardio is the appropriate cardiovascular fat loss tool.** At Zone 2 intensity — 60–75% of maximum heart rate — fat oxidation is actually higher as a percentage of total fuel use than at HIIT intensities. This is because at very high intensities, the body relies predominantly on carbohydrate (glycogen) for fuel, as fat oxidation cannot keep pace with the energy demand. Zone 2 work, sustained for 30–45 minutes, produces substantial total fat oxidation, a manageable cortisol response, and no thermoregulatory crisis. It is already programmed into this client's plan and can be modestly increased in volume if fat loss is a priority.

**Protein intake is the nutritional fat loss tool.** The nutrition plan already prescribes 1.8–2.2 g of protein per kilogram of bodyweight per day. This level of protein intake has a meaningful thermogenic effect — the thermic effect of protein is 20–30% of its caloric content, compared to 5–10% for carbohydrates and 0–3% for fat. It also preserves lean mass during any caloric deficit, ensuring that weight lost comes from fat rather than muscle. If your client is not consistently hitting her protein targets, closing that gap will have a more meaningful impact on body composition than adding fasted HIIT.

**A modest, sustainable caloric deficit is the energy balance tool.** A deficit of 200–300 kcal per day — achieved through a combination of slightly reduced caloric intake and the caloric expenditure of the existing training programme — will produce meaningful fat loss over 12 weeks without the hormonal disruption of aggressive restriction or fasted high-intensity training. This deficit should never come from reducing protein. It should come from modest reductions in refined carbohydrates and added fats, while maintaining the nutrient density of the overall diet.

**Sleep is the underrated fat loss tool.** Poor sleep — which your client is already experiencing due to vasomotor symptoms — directly dysregulates the appetite hormones ghrelin and leptin, increasing hunger and reducing satiety signalling. It also elevates cortisol, promoting fat storage. Every intervention that improves your client's sleep quality — the magnesium supplementation in the nutrition plan, the evening flexibility sessions, the cooling protocol, the avoidance of late-day caffeine — is also a fat loss intervention. This is worth communicating explicitly to your client, because it reframes sleep management as an active part of her fat loss strategy rather than a passive health consideration.

---

## What Can Be Added: Fed, Cooled, Timed HIIT

While fasted morning HIIT is contraindicated, HIIT itself is not permanently off the table for this client. The Phase 2 cardio programme already introduces structured high-intensity intervals in a controlled format. These can be progressed and, if your client's vasomotor symptoms improve over the course of the programme — which regular exercise, improved sleep, and better nutrition often produce — the scope for higher-intensity work increases.

The conditions under which HIIT is appropriate for this client are specific and non-negotiable:

**Fed state:** A meal or substantial snack containing at least 25 g of protein and 30 g of carbohydrate must have been consumed within 60–90 minutes before the session. This is not optional.

**Cooled environment:** Air-conditioned gym with confirmed temperature below 20°C, or outdoor training before 8:00 am in spring or autumn only. Not during June through August outdoors.

**Appropriate timing:** Not first thing in the morning when cortisol is at its diurnal peak. Mid-morning (10:00–11:00 am) or late afternoon (16:00–18:00 pm) are the optimal windows, as cortisol is lower and the body is better prepared to manage the stress response.

**Not on resistance training days:** HIIT and heavy resistance training compete for recovery resources. They should not share a day.

**Readiness score 19 or above:** Below this threshold, HIIT is replaced with Zone 2 work.

**Cooling protocol in full:** Cooling towel, cold water, fan, extended post-session cool-down.

Under these conditions, the structured intervals already programmed in Phase 2 and Phase 3 of the cardio plan represent the appropriate HIIT dose for this client. They are not fasted, not in the morning heat, and not layered on top of an already demanding resistance programme without recovery consideration.

## How to Have This Conversation With Your Client

Your client has come to you with a specific request based on something she has heard or read. The fasted morning HIIT for fat loss idea is everywhere in fitness culture, and it is not unreasonable that she has encountered it and found it compelling. The way you handle this conversation will determine whether she trusts your clinical judgement or goes and does it anyway without telling you.

The following framing is suggested.

Acknowledge the goal first and take it seriously. Fat loss is a legitimate objective and one the programme can support. Do not make her feel that the goal itself is problematic.

Explain the GP restriction clearly and without hedging. The restriction on fasted HIIT in heat is not your preference or your caution — it is a clinical instruction from her doctor, based on her specific physiology. You are not in a position to override it, and doing so would be outside your scope of practice. This is a factual statement, not a negotiation.

Explain why the restriction exists in terms she can understand. The narrowed thermoneutral zone, the cortisol awakening response, the interaction between heat and vasomotor symptoms — these can be explained in plain language without being condescending. Most clients respond well to understanding the mechanism behind a restriction rather than simply being told no.

Reframe the fat loss strategy around what works. Show her the evidence that fasted HIIT does not produce superior fat loss outcomes compared to fed training when total calories are matched. Show her that the programme she is already doing — progressive resistance training, Zone 2 cardio, high protein intake, sleep optimisation — is a more effective fat loss strategy for her specific physiology than fasted HIIT would be.

Offer the fed, cooled, timed HIIT option as a genuine alternative. She is not being denied high-intensity work. She is being given high-intensity work in a format that is safe and effective for her. The Phase 2 and Phase 3 interval sessions are genuinely hard. Present them as such.

Finally, suggest she raises the fat loss goal explicitly with her GP at her next appointment. If her GP agrees that additional high-intensity work is appropriate and wants to modify the exercise restrictions, that conversation should happen in a clinical setting with full knowledge of her current programme. Your role is to work within the clinical parameters you have been given, not to circumvent them.

# 1RM Testing at End of Phase 3: Clinical Assessment & Protocol

**Week 12 | 27 July – 21 August 2026**
**Full Perimenopause & Vasomotor Symptom Considerations**

---

## Direct Answer First

Yes, with conditions. A 1RM test at the end of Phase 3 is appropriate for this client and is consistent with her profile as an advanced lifter. It is also clinically defensible given the GP clearance for full resistance training. However, a 1RM test for a perimenopausal woman with significant vasomotor symptoms is not the same procedure as a 1RM test for a younger athlete without these considerations, and running it as though it were would be a mistake.

The conditions under which the test proceeds, the modifications to standard 1RM testing protocol, the specific safety provisions for vasomotor symptom management, and the decision framework for postponing or abandoning the test are all detailed below. If these conditions are met, your client has every reason to expect a safe, valid, and motivating testing experience that reflects twelve weeks of serious work.

---

## Why 1RM Testing Is Appropriate for This Client

### She Has Earned It Physiologically

The programme has been structured specifically to prepare your client for near-maximal loading. Phase 1 established movement quality and connective tissue tolerance. Phase 2 revised pushed intensity to 90% of estimated 1RM in Week 7, meaning your client has already performed sets at near-maximal loads under controlled conditions. Phase 3 has consolidated this with sustained high-intensity work across four weeks. A 1RM test at the end of this progression is not a leap into the unknown — it is a logical and well-prepared endpoint.

The wave loading structure of Phase 2 revised and the progressive intensity of Phase 3 mean that your client's nervous system has been systematically trained to recruit motor units at near-maximal levels. The 1RM test asks her to extend this to true maximum. The physiological gap between 90% and 100% of 1RM is smaller than the gap between any other adjacent decile, and she has been working in that territory for weeks.

### Bone Health Context Makes It Valuable

The GP clearance for full resistance training was given in the context of bone density. Maximal and near-maximal loading produces the greatest osteogenic stimulus of any resistance training intensity — the mechanical strain on bone at 1RM loads is substantially greater than at 75–80% loads. A successful 1RM test is therefore not just a performance metric. It is a bone health intervention in its own right, and documenting the loads achieved provides a baseline for future programming decisions that will continue to serve her skeletal health.

### Psychological Value Is Clinically Relevant

Perimenopause is frequently accompanied by a loss of confidence in the body — a sense that the body is becoming less reliable, less predictable, and less capable. This is understandable given the symptom burden your client is carrying. A successful 1RM test, demonstrating objectively that she is stronger than she was twelve weeks ago, is a meaningful counter-narrative to that experience. The psychological benefit of this kind of concrete, measurable achievement should not be dismissed as merely motivational. Self-efficacy — the belief in one's capacity to perform — is a genuine determinant of long-term exercise adherence, and exercise adherence is one of the most important factors in long-term health outcomes for perimenopausal women.

---

## What Will Be Tested

Not every lift in the programme is appropriate for 1RM testing. The selection criteria are: movement pattern safety at maximal load, relevance to the programme's primary training goals, and practical testability within a single session without excessive fatigue accumulation.

**Lifts selected for 1RM testing:**

**Back Squat.** The primary lower body strength exercise of the programme and the most important test of lower body maximal strength. Well-suited to 1RM testing in an advanced lifter with established technique.

**Barbell Bench Press.** The primary upper body pushing exercise. Standard 1RM test with a spotter. Straightforward and appropriate.

**Trap Bar Deadlift.** Selected over the conventional deadlift for two reasons. First, the trap bar has been the primary deadlift variation throughout the programme, meaning the 1RM test reflects actual training adaptation rather than a movement pattern that has been trained less specifically. Second, the trap bar's more upright torso position reduces lumbar shear force at maximal loads, making it the safer choice for a 1RM attempt in a client whose connective tissue is operating in a lower-oestrogen environment.

**Lifts not selected for 1RM testing:**

The bent-over row, overhead press, Romanian deadlift, and all accessory exercises are excluded from 1RM testing. The bent-over row and Romanian deadlift carry significant lumbar loading at maximal efforts that is not justified by the testing value. The overhead press is excluded because maximal overhead loading in a fatigued state carries shoulder injury risk that outweighs the informational value of the test. These lifts will continue to be progressed in any subsequent programming based on the working loads achieved in Phase 3.

---

## Testing Session Structure

### Scheduling Within Week 12

Week 12 is the final week of the programme. The 1RM testing is distributed across two sessions rather than compressed into one. Attempting to test squat, bench press, and trap bar deadlift in a single session would produce fatigue-compromised results on the later lifts and would represent an inappropriate total physiological stress for this client.

**Recommended Week 12 Schedule:**

| Day | Session |
|---|---|
| Monday | Lower Body 1RM Test: Back Squat + Trap Bar Deadlift |
| Tuesday | Rest — complete rest, no cardio, no flexibility session |
| Wednesday | Upper Body 1RM Test: Barbell Bench Press |
| Thursday | Rest |
| Friday | Optional: Programme Completion Session (light, celebratory) |
| Saturday | Optional: Zone 1 cardio or flexibility session |
| Sunday | Rest |

**Why Monday and Wednesday?** The two-day gap between lower and upper body testing allows partial recovery of the nervous system and the lower body musculature between sessions without allowing so much time that the testing momentum is lost. Tuesday is a complete rest day — no cardio, no flexibility work, no activity that adds meaningful physiological stress. The nervous system needs this day.

**Why not test all three lifts on Monday?** Squatting and deadlifting to a true 1RM in the same session is physiologically possible but produces a meaningful compromise in one or both results. The squat fatigues the posterior chain and the nervous system in ways that directly impair deadlift performance, and vice versa. Separating them within the same session by 30–45 minutes of rest reduces but does not eliminate this interference. Given that the purpose of the test is to obtain valid maximal strength data, separating the lower body tests into squat first and deadlift second within the Monday session — with a minimum 20-minute rest between final attempts — is the appropriate compromise between session efficiency and result validity.

---

## Pre-Testing Conditions and Go/No-Go Criteria

This is the most important section of this document. A 1RM test is a maximal physiological effort. For this client, the interaction between maximal effort, vasomotor symptoms, and the hormonal environment of perimenopause means that the decision to proceed must be made on the day, based on objective criteria, not on the basis of the schedule alone.

### The Go/No-Go Framework

Assess the following on the morning of each testing session. This assessment should be completed at least 2 hours before the session begins, giving time to make and act on the decision.

**Mandatory Go criteria — all must be met:**

**Readiness score 20 or above.** This is a higher threshold than the 17–19 required for elevated-intensity resistance training in Phase 2. A 1RM test is a greater physiological and psychological demand than a working set at 90% 1RM, and the readiness threshold reflects this. If the readiness score is 17–19, the session defaults to a heavy working session at 90–92% of estimated 1RM rather than a true 1RM attempt. This is not a failed test day — it is a sensible decision that protects the validity of the eventual test.

**Sleep: minimum 7 hours the preceding night.** Sleep is the single most important determinant of maximal strength expression on a given day. The nervous system's capacity to recruit motor units at maximal levels is directly impaired by sleep deprivation. If your client has had fewer than 7 hours of sleep — whether due to vasomotor symptoms, life stress, or any other cause — postpone the test by 24–48 hours. This is a non-negotiable criterion.

**No severe hot flash episode in the preceding 4 hours.** A severe vasomotor episode in the hours before a 1RM test indicates that the hypothalamic thermoregulatory system is already under significant stress. Adding the core temperature rise and cardiovascular demand of a maximal lift to this state is inappropriate. A mild or moderate flash that has fully resolved is acceptable. A severe episode that has occurred within 4 hours is a postponement criterion.

**Fed state confirmed.** Your client must have eaten a pre-testing meal containing at least 30 g of protein and 40–50 g of carbohydrate within 90 minutes of the session start. This is more substantial than the standard pre-training meal because the glycolytic and neuromuscular demands of 1RM testing are higher than working sets. A small amount of caffeine — one cup of coffee or tea — is acceptable and may modestly enhance maximal strength expression, but only if your client regularly uses caffeine and it does not worsen her vasomotor symptoms. Do not introduce caffeine on testing day if she does not normally use it.

**Gym temperature confirmed below 20°C.** The testing environment must be actively cooled. Confirm this before your client arrives, not when she is already warming up. If the gym cannot be cooled to below 20°C on the testing day, postpone. This is not negotiable.

**No lower body resistance training in the preceding 72 hours (for Monday squat/deadlift test).** The final lower body resistance session of Phase 3 should be completed no later than the preceding Thursday, giving a minimum of 72 hours of lower body recovery before Monday's test. If Phase 3 Week 11 has run to schedule, this will be the case automatically.

**No upper body resistance training in the preceding 48 hours (for Wednesday bench press test).** The Monday lower body test does not significantly fatigue the upper body, so 48 hours is sufficient recovery before Wednesday's bench press test.

---

### Postponement Protocol

If any mandatory Go criterion is not met, the test is postponed. Postponement is not failure — it is good clinical practice. The following postponement options are available:

**24-hour postponement:** If the issue is sleep quality or a recent vasomotor episode, postpone by 24 hours and reassess. The revised schedule becomes Tuesday lower body, Thursday upper body.

**48-hour postponement:** If the issue is more significant — a cluster of poor readiness scores, a difficult symptom period, or an environmental issue with the gym — postpone by 48 hours. Revised schedule: Wednesday lower body, Friday upper body.

**Full week postponement:** If your client is in a high-symptom period that has persisted for several days, postpone the entire testing week by one week. This extends the programme to 13 weeks but produces a valid test result rather than a compromised one. A compromised 1RM test is worse than no test at all, because it produces inaccurate baseline data that will mislead future programming.

## 1RM Testing Protocol: Session by Session

### Monday — Lower Body Testing Session

**Arrival and environment check (15 minutes before session start):**
Confirm gym temperature. Ensure cooling towel, minimum 750 ml cold water, and fan are in place at the rack and platform. Your client should arrive having completed her readiness assessment and pre-testing meal. Take 5 minutes to discuss the plan for the session — which lifts, in which order, what the warm-up progression looks like, and what the abort criteria are. This conversation serves both a practical and a psychological function: it reduces anxiety, establishes shared expectations, and ensures your client knows she has explicit permission to stop at any point without it being a failure.

**General warm-up (10 minutes):**

5 minutes of easy cycling or rowing at Zone 1 intensity. Heart rate should reach 95–100 bpm by the end of this period. The purpose is to raise tissue temperature, increase joint lubrication, and begin the cardiovascular warm-up without generating significant fatigue or core temperature rise. Monitor for vasomotor symptoms throughout. If a hot flash occurs during the general warm-up, pause, apply cooling towel, sip cold water, and wait for full resolution before continuing. Do not rush through a flash to get to the lifting.

Hip 90/90 mobility: 60 seconds each side.
Glute bridges: 15 repetitions.
Banded clamshells: 15 repetitions each side.
World's Greatest Stretch: 5 repetitions each side.
Ankle dorsiflexion mobilisation: 10 repetitions each side.

**Back Squat 1RM Attempt:**

The warm-up progression for the 1RM attempt is the most important technical element of the testing protocol. Too few warm-up sets and the nervous system is not adequately prepared for maximal loading. Too many warm-up sets and fatigue accumulates before the true attempt. The following progression is calibrated for an advanced lifter whose estimated 1RM is known from Phase 3 working loads.

Estimating the target 1RM: Use the loads achieved in Phase 3 Week 11 as the basis. If your client completed 4 sets of 2 reps at 90% of her estimated 1RM in Week 11, her true 1RM is likely 5–8% above her Week 11 working load, accounting for the fact that Week 11 sets were not taken to failure. Set the target 1RM attempt at the lower end of this range for the first attempt, with a second attempt planned at the upper end if the first is successful.

*Warm-up set progression:*

| Set | Load | Reps | Rest After |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 40% estimated 1RM | 8 | 2 minutes |
| 2 | 55% estimated 1RM | 5 | 2 minutes |
| 3 | 68% estimated 1RM | 3 | 3 minutes |
| 4 | 78% estimated 1RM | 2 | 3 minutes |
| 5 | 85% estimated 1RM | 1 | 4 minutes |
| 6 | 92% estimated 1RM | 1 | 5 minutes |
| 7 | First 1RM attempt | 1 | 5–8 minutes if second attempt planned |

Each warm-up set should feel progressively more demanding but never maximal. Bar speed should be good through Set 5. Set 6 at 92% will feel heavy — this is expected and appropriate. The 5-minute rest after Set 6 is the most important rest period of the session. Use it fully. Your client should be seated, applying the cooling towel if needed, sipping cold water, and mentally preparing for the attempt. Do not fill this rest period with coaching cues, conversation, or distraction. She needs to be internally focused.

*The 1RM attempt:*

Approach the bar with the same pre-lift routine your client uses for every heavy set — the same breath, the same brace, the same walkout. Consistency of pre-lift routine is associated with better maximal performance because it activates the same neuromuscular preparation sequence that has been rehearsed across hundreds of training sessions.

Descent: controlled, same tempo as training. Do not rush the descent on a 1RM attempt — a controlled descent loads the stretch-shortening cycle more effectively and produces a better drive out of the bottom.

Drive: maximal intent from the bottom. The cue that works best for most advanced squatters at maximal loads is to think about driving the floor away rather than standing up — this maintains the posterior chain engagement and prevents the forward lean that commonly occurs when the load is very heavy.

Lockout: complete the rep to full hip and knee extension. A 1RM that does not reach full lockout is not a valid 1RM.

*Spotter protocol:* Two spotters are strongly preferred for the back squat 1RM attempt — one on each side of the bar. If only one spotter is available, a squat rack with properly set safety bars is mandatory. The safety bars should be set at a height that catches the bar if your client fails the rep, without being so high that they interfere with the bottom position of a successful rep. Test this height during the warm-up sets.

*If the first attempt is successful:* Rest 5–8 minutes. Increase the load by 2–4% for the second attempt. This is a conservative increment — the goal is a successful second attempt, not a maximal increment. A successful second attempt at a modest increment is more valuable than a failed attempt at an aggressive increment, both for the data it produces and for your client's psychological experience of the test.

*If the first attempt fails:* Assess where the failure occurred. If the rep was missed in the bottom position (could not initiate the drive), the load was too heavy and the true 1RM is below the attempted weight. Reduce by 3–5% and attempt again after 8 minutes. If the rep was missed mid-way up (initiated the drive but could not complete it), the load may be at or very close to the true 1RM. Reduce by 1–2% and attempt again after 8 minutes. If the rep was missed at lockout (nearly complete but could not finish), the load is very close to the true 1RM and the attempt counts as a near-miss. The true 1RM is likely within 1–2% of the attempted weight.

*Maximum three attempts at or above 90% of estimated 1RM.* Beyond three near-maximal attempts, fatigue and nervous system depletion will compromise both the validity of subsequent attempts and the recovery available for the deadlift portion of the session.

**Rest between squat and deadlift testing: minimum 20 minutes.**

This is a genuine rest period. Your client should be seated in a cool area, not standing, not moving around the gym, not performing mobility work. Sip cold water. Apply cooling towel if needed. Eat a small carbohydrate snack — 20–30 g of fast-acting carbohydrate such as a banana, a handful of dates, or a sports gel — to partially replenish glycogen before the deadlift attempts. This is the one context in the programme where a fast-acting carbohydrate snack mid-session is specifically recommended.

Monitor for vasomotor symptoms during this rest period. If a significant hot flash occurs, extend the rest period until full resolution plus an additional 5 minutes. Do not begin deadlift warm-ups during or immediately after a flash.

**Trap Bar Deadlift 1RM Attempt:**

The deadlift warm-up progression is abbreviated compared to the squat progression, because the general warm-up and squat warm-up sets have already elevated tissue temperature and prepared the nervous system. Fewer warm-up sets are needed, but the rest periods remain generous.

*Warm-up set progression:*

| Set | Load | Reps | Rest After |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 50% estimated 1RM | 5 | 2 minutes |
| 2 | 65% estimated 1RM | 3 | 3 minutes |
| 3 | 78% estimated 1RM | 2 | 3 minutes |
| 4 | 88% estimated 1RM | 1 | 5 minutes |

*The 1RM attempt:*

Setup is everything in the trap bar deadlift. Feet centred in the trap bar, hip-width apart. Hinge to the handles, grip firmly, set the lats by thinking about protecting the armpits. Take a full diaphragmatic breath, brace the entire trunk — 360 degrees of pressure, not just the front — and drive the floor away. The trap bar deadlift should feel like a leg press with the bar in the hands, not a back exercise.

The most common technical failure at maximal trap bar deadlift loads is losing the lat engagement and allowing the upper back to round, which shifts the load to the lumbar spine. Watch for this specifically. If upper back rounding occurs on the first attempt, it is a technique cue issue rather than a strength issue — the load may be appropriate but the setup needs reinforcing before the second attempt.

*Same attempt protocol as the squat:* Maximum three attempts at or above 90% of estimated 1RM. If the first attempt is successful, rest 5–8 minutes and increase by 2–4% for the second attempt.

**Post-session protocol:**

Do not rush the post-session cool-down after a 1RM testing session. Your client's core temperature will be elevated, her cardiovascular system will be under significant demand, and the risk of a vasomotor episode is high in the immediate post-session period. The following applies:

5 minutes of very easy walking — not stretching, not mobility work, just gentle movement to begin the cardiovascular cool-down.

Seated rest for 10 minutes in a cool environment. Cold water with electrolytes. Cooling towel to the back of the neck and wrists. Fan directed at the body.

Post-session meal within 45 minutes: minimum 40 g of protein and 60–80 g of carbohydrate. This is the most important post-session meal of the entire 12-week programme. The physiological stress of 1RM testing — the nervous system demand, the muscle fibre recruitment, the hormonal response — creates a significant recovery requirement that must be met nutritionally.

Record all results immediately: loads attempted, loads achieved, number of attempts, any technical observations, readiness score, vasomotor symptom occurrence during session. This data is the primary output of the testing day and should be documented before your client leaves the gym.

### Wednesday — Upper Body Testing Session

**Pre-session assessment:**

Repeat the full Go/No-Go assessment on Wednesday morning. Do not assume that a successful Monday session means Wednesday is automatically a Go. Your client may have had poor sleep on Monday night due to the physiological arousal of the testing session, or vasomotor symptoms may have been worsened by the Monday stress response. Assess independently.

**General warm-up (8 minutes):**

5 minutes easy cycling or rowing at Zone 1.
Band pull-aparts: 25 repetitions.
Shoulder CARs: 5 circles each direction each shoulder.
Scapular push-ups: 10 repetitions.
Face pulls with light resistance: 20 repetitions.

The upper body warm-up is slightly shorter than the lower body warm-up because the cardiovascular and tissue temperature demands of bench press testing are lower than those of squat and deadlift testing. The shoulder-specific warm-up is more detailed, reflecting the importance of rotator cuff preparation before maximal pressing loads.

**Barbell Bench Press 1RM Attempt:**

*Warm-up set progression:*

| Set | Load | Reps | Rest After |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 40% estimated 1RM | 8 | 90 seconds |
| 2 | 55% estimated 1RM | 5 | 2 minutes |
| 3 | 68% estimated 1RM | 3 | 2.5 minutes |

| 5 | 85% estimated 1RM | 1 | 4 minutes |
| 6 | 92% estimated 1RM | 1 | 5 minutes |
| 7 | First 1RM attempt | 1 | 5–8 minutes if second attempt planned |

*The 1RM attempt:*

Setup: feet flat on the floor, back in a natural arch (not an exaggerated powerlifting arch — a comfortable, stable position), shoulder blades retracted and depressed into the bench, grip just outside shoulder width. The setup should be identical to every bench press set your client has performed across the 12-week programme. Consistency of setup is as important for the 1RM attempt as it is for any working set.

Descent: controlled, 2–3 seconds, bar path slightly diagonal — not straight down to the chest, but angling slightly toward the lower chest as the elbows track at approximately 45–60 degrees from the torso. This bar path reduces shoulder joint stress at the bottom position and is the mechanically optimal path for most lifters.

Touch and drive: the bar touches the chest — it does not bounce, it does not pause for more than a fraction of a second. Drive explosively upward, maintaining the bar path in reverse. The drive should feel like pushing yourself into the bench as much as pushing the bar away from the chest.

*Spotter protocol:* A spotter is mandatory for the bench press 1RM attempt. The spotter stands behind the bench, hands close to but not touching the bar throughout the lift, ready to assist immediately if the bar stalls or begins to descend.

**Client: Female, 47 | Advanced Lifter | Early Perimenopause**

## Master Reference Document

This summary consolidates every component of the programme into a single navigable reference. It is designed to be used session by session across the twelve weeks. ## Standing Protocols (Apply Every Session, Every Week)

### Readiness Score (Complete Before Every Session)

Rate each item 1–5 (1 = very poor/severe, 5 = excellent/none):
1. Sleep quality
2. Energy level
3. Hot flash severity last 24 hours
4. Joint comfort
5. Mood and motivation

**20–25:** Full prescription.
**13–19:** Lower end of intensity range. Reduce top sets 5–10%. Prioritise technique.
**Below 13:** Movement quality session only. 60–65% of working weights. Cut volume by one third.

### Cooling Protocol (Every Session)

- Cold water minimum 750 ml present at all times.
- Cooling towel at rack, bench, or cardio equipment.
- Fan or air conditioning confirmed before session begins.
- Session scheduled before 11:00 am or after 17:00 pm June through August.
- Gym temperature below 20°C for all elevated-intensity sessions.
- If hot flash occurs mid-set: pause or abandon set. Do not increase load on next set. Resume when fully resolved.
- Post-session: 10-minute cool-down walk, cold shower or cool-water face and neck wash within 20 minutes, 500 ml water with electrolytes within 30 minutes.

### Pre-Session Nutrition (Every Session)

- Meal or snack containing minimum 25 g protein and 30 g carbohydrate within 60–90 minutes before training.
- No fasted sessions of any kind.
- Collagen peptides 10–15 g with 50–100 mg vitamin C 30–60 minutes before training.

### Week 4 — Deload (22–28 June 2026)

**Resistance:** Reduce all loads by 15–20% from Week 3. Reduce all sets by one. Maintain full range of motion and movement quality throughout. Introduce 30-second isometric holds at the most challenging joint angle of each main lift warm-up.

**Cardio:** Return to Week 1 parameters. Zone 2 for 25 minutes on Wednesday. Zone 1 for 30 minutes on Saturday.

**Flexibility:** Maintain Tuesday and Friday evening sessions and Sunday session at normal prescription. These are recovery tools and are not reduced during the deload.

| Bench Press | 55–58% 1RM × 4 × 5 |
| Trap Bar Deadlift | 58–60% 1RM × 3 × 5 |
| Romanian Deadlift | 55% 1RM × 2 × 8 |

**Week 4 Review Checklist:**
- Review readiness scores from Weeks 1–3. Identify patterns.
- Identify which cardio modalities produced fewest vasomotor episodes.
- Confirm nutrition targets are being met consistently.
- Assess flexibility session compliance and any areas of persistent restriction.
- Set Phase 2 working weight targets based on Week 3 loads.
